Looking at the log, four of your nine tools are actually broken, and two more (dots_ocr, qwen25_vl_7b) are inconclusive because the harness swallows the real traceback (hyp, err = "", str(e) only stores str(e), no traceback.format_exc()). Here's what's actually going on with each, checked against current package state (Aug 2026):

1. unlimited_ocr — confirmed root cause
cannot import name 'is_torch_fx_available' from 'transformers.utils.import_utils' is a known breaking change: transformers v5.0 removed that function entirely, and Baidu's modeling_deepseek_v2.py (pulled in via trust_remote_code) still imports it directly. Your setup cell pins "transformers>=4.49.0", which now resolves to v5.x and breaks. Fix — either pin transformers below v5, or monkeypatch the missing symbol back before loading (safer, since Qwen2.5-VL may want newer transformers):

import transformers.utils.import_utils as _iu
if not hasattr(_iu, "is_torch_fx_available"):
    _iu.is_torch_fx_available = lambda: True  # torch.fx is always available on torch>=2.1
    import transformers.utils as _u
    _u.is_torch_fx_available = _iu.is_torch_fx_available

Run this once, before calling unlimited_ocr_load().

2. paddleocr_vl — confirmed root cause (message is deliberately generic)
That "A dependency error occurred during pipeline creation" text is PaddleX's DependencyError, and it's known to hide the actual missing package. It almost always means the paddlex[ocr] (or paddleocr[doc-parser]) extras weren't pulled in — plain pip install paddleocr doesn't install everything PaddleOCRVL needs. Fix your setup cell:

!pip install -q "paddleocr[doc-parser]" "paddlex[ocr]"

And to actually see what's missing next time (rather than the wrapped message), catch it explicitly in the load wrapper:

def paddleocr_vl_load():
    from paddleocr import PaddleOCRVL
    try:
        return PaddleOCRVL(pipeline_version="v1.5")
    except Exception:
        import traceback; traceback.print_exc()
        raise

3. surya — confirmed root cause: you're on Surya 2, the old API is gone
surya-ocr did a ground-up rewrite. RecognitionPredictor/DetectionPredictor no longer take a plain constructor + det_predictor= kwarg — recognition, layout, and OCR now go through a single VLM served by vLLM (GPU) or llama.cpp (CPU/Apple), spun up via a SuryaInferenceManager. That's almost certainly why every page in your run errored. New wrapper:

def surya_load():
    from surya.inference import SuryaInferenceManager
    from surya.recognition import RecognitionPredictor
    manager = SuryaInferenceManager()          # auto-spawns vllm or llama-server
    rec = RecognitionPredictor(manager)
    return rec

def surya_predict(handle, pil_img):
    preds = handle([pil_img.convert("RGB")])
    page = preds[0]
    # v2 schema: text_lines -> blocks (HTML), not .text_lines
    return "\n".join(b.get("text", "") for b in page.blocks) if hasattr(page, "blocks") else str(page)

Practical Kaggle concern worth flagging before you spend time on this: the manager auto-spawning a vLLM server (which itself needs Docker + NVIDIA Container Toolkit) inside a Kaggle notebook container is likely to be fragile or outright unsupported — Kaggle doesn't give you Docker-in-Docker. You may need to force the llama.cpp CPU backend instead (SURYA_INFERENCE_BACKEND=llamacpp env var) even though you have GPUs, or drop Surya from this bake-off if it can't run cleanly in that environment.

4. dots_ocr — can't diagnose from what's shown; the traceback got eaten
Model loaded fine (the flash attention not available lines are just warnings, not the failure), but all 45 pages still errored. Your loop only stores str(e) and never prints it, so the log you pasted doesn't actually contain the reason. Before I guess at a fix, add this and rerun just this model:

except Exception as e:
    import traceback; traceback.print_exc()
    hyp, err = "", str(e)

Then run bakeoff_df[bakeoff_df.tool == "dots_ocr"].error.iloc[0] and share it. My best guesses in order of likelihood: apply_chat_template on dots.ocr's processor doesn't accept the generic {"type":"image","image": PIL.Image} content dict the way Qwen's does (dots.ocr's official usage passes a file path or a specific image-token prompt format rather than routing through the standard chat-template image slot), or the custom processor expects images= to be a nested list matching a different bbox/layout output schema.

5. qwen25_vl_7b — log is just truncated, not necessarily failed
The pasted log ends mid-download (tokenizer.json: 7.03M/? ...) with no done: or LOAD FAILED line after it — that's the log cutting off, not evidence of an error. Paste the rest if it did fail.

Want me to also add a global fix to bakeoff_records so every future error captures the full traceback instead of just str(e) — that'll save you from this same "which model actually failed and why" guessing game next run?

Diagnosed Docker constraint and pivoted to llama.cpp backend solution.

That traceback is unambiguous: Surya 2's vllm backend needs a running Docker daemon to spawn its inference server, and Kaggle notebook containers don't have Docker available inside them (no nested Docker). So this isn't a bug in your wrapper — the manager auto-selected the GPU-oriented vllm backend because it saw your T4s, then failed at the docker binary check.

Fix: force the llama.cpp backend instead, which runs as a plain binary (no Docker) and works fine on Kaggle.

1. Confirm the exact setting name before trusting my guess — settings.py is the source of truth, not the README:

!python -c "import surya.settings as s, inspect; print(inspect.getsource(s))" | grep -i -A2 -B2 "backend\|llama"

2. Install the llama.cpp server binary (portable, no Docker/root needed — grab the CPU build to sidestep the CUDA-version mismatches you're already hitting with onnxruntime):

!wget -q -O /tmp/llama.zip $(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/latest \
    | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print([a['browser_download_url'] for a in d['assets'] if 'ubuntu' in a['name'] and 'cuda' not in a['name']][0])")
!unzip -q /tmp/llama.zip -d /opt/llama.cpp
!chmod +x /opt/llama.cpp/llama-server 2>/dev/null || find /opt/llama.cpp -name "llama-server" -exec chmod +x {} \;

(Check the extracted folder for where llama-server actually landed — release zip layouts shift between versions — and adjust the chmod/PATH line to match.)

3. Point Surya at it and force the backend, before calling surya_load():

import os
os.environ["PATH"] += os.pathsep + "/opt/llama.cpp"
os.environ["SURYA_INFERENCE_BACKEND"] = "llamacpp"  # verify exact value from step 1

If step 1 shows a different literal (e.g. "llama_cpp" or "llama.cpp"), use that instead — settings enums like this often don't match the prose in the README exactly.

One more thing worth deciding up front: even with llama.cpp working, you're now running Surya's OCR through CPU inference across 45+ pages per sweep step, which will be dramatically slower than the other models in your bake-off (and the accuracy-vs-latency scatter plot in cell c600147b will make that obvious). Given the trouble this model is causing, it might be worth asking yourself whether it's worth keeping in the Tier-1 bake-off at all versus just noting in your write-up that Surya 2's architecture change made it impractical for this environment — that's a legitimate finding too, and the apsisnet_bbocr CUDA warning you're also seeing repeatedly (harmless, it's already falling back to CPU successfully) suggests this Kaggle image is generally behind on CUDA/onnxruntime version alignment, which will bite you again if you keep leaning on GPU-dependent backends.

got_ocr2 — straightforward. The custom modeling file imports verovio (a music-notation library GOT-OCR2 bundles for sheet-music transcription) even though you don't need that feature:

!pip install -q verovio

dots_ocr — the model's processor emits an mm_token_type_ids tensor that model.generate()'s kwarg validator doesn't recognize on this transformers version. Drop it before calling generate:

inputs = processor(text=[text_prompt], images=[pil_img.convert("RGB")], return_tensors="pt").to("cuda:0")
inputs.pop("mm_token_type_ids", None)   # <-- add this line
with torch.no_grad():
    gen_ids = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2048, do_sample=False)

qwen25_vl_7b's OOM — this is actually the most important find. Look at the numbers: "12.46 GiB memory in use" before Qwen even starts loading. Qwen runs right after dots_ocr in your registry, and I think your bake-off loop has a real reference leak. In cell e82c82b3:

try:
    handle = load_fn()
except Exception as e:
    ...
...
try:
    unload_fn(handle)
except Exception:
    pass
free_gpu()

unload_fn(handle) does del handle — but that only deletes the local name inside dots_ocr_unload(). The outer handle variable in this loop still holds a live reference to the ~6GB dots_ocr model object, so free_gpu()'s gc.collect() has nothing to collect — the object isn't actually released until the next iteration's handle = load_fn() line runs (and even then, Python evaluates the right-hand side first, so the new model tries to allocate GPU memory while the old one is still resident). That's consistent with Qwen failing to fit a 5GB allocation on a 14.56GB T4 that already had 12.46GB in use before it started. Fix:

try:
    unload_fn(handle)
except Exception:
    pass
del handle          # <-- drop the outer-scope reference too
free_gpu()

Worth adding gpu_mem_report(tool_name) right after this to confirm memory actually drops to ~0 between models — cheap insurance against this happening again with a model further down the registry.

surya — still the same Docker requirement from before; nothing new in this traceback. The llama.cpp-backend fix from my previous message stands, but it's setup work (downloading the binary, setting env vars), not a one-line patch.

Needs more diagnosis (traceback still hidden)

paddleocr_vl — identical generic DependencyError as your first run, meaning the pip install "paddleocr[doc-parser]" "paddlex[ocr]" fix either wasn't applied yet or didn't resolve it. Before guessing further, get the real underlying package name — PaddleX's error wrapper hides it:

except Exception:

The __cause__ chain in a full traceback (not just the wrapped RuntimeError) should name the actual missing module.

unlimited_ocr — this is a new failure, meaning your is_torch_fx_available monkeypatch worked and you got past the transformers v5 import error, but hit a second, different incompatibility: 'UnlimitedOCRConfig' object has no attribute 'pad_token_id'. This is happening inside AutoModel.from_pretrained(...), but your load try/except only captured str(e), not the full trace, so I can't yet tell whether it's DeepSeek-V2 config init code doing self.config.pad_token_id without a getattr(..., default) guard, or something in generation-config setup. Add the same traceback.print_exc() pattern to the load except block (not just predict) to get the real call site — right now every LOAD FAILED line in your failed_models dict is diagnostically useless beyond the top-level message.

Once you've got those two tracebacks, send them over and I'll pin down the exact fixes rather than guessing at config internals blind.

---- 5.2 EasyOCR ------------------------------------------------------------

def easyocr_load():
    import easyocr
    return easyocr.Reader(["bn"], gpu=torch.cuda.is_available())
def easyocr_unload(handle):
    del handle
    free_gpu()
def easyocr_predict(handle, pil_img: Image.Image) -> str:
    arr = np.array(pil_img.convert("RGB"))
    result = handle.readtext(arr, detail=0, paragraph=True)
    return "\n".join(result)

---- 5.3 Surya OCR -----------------------------------------------------------

def surya_load():
    from surya.inference import SuryaInferenceManager
    from surya.recognition import RecognitionPredictor
    manager = SuryaInferenceManager()          # auto-spawns vllm or llama-server
    rec = RecognitionPredictor(manager)
    return rec
def surya_predict(handle, pil_img):
    preds = handle([pil_img.convert("RGB")])
    page = preds[0]
    # v2 schema: text_lines -> blocks (HTML), not .text_lines
    return "\n".join(b.get("text", "") for b in page.blocks) if hasattr(page, "blocks") else str(page)
def surya_unload(handle):
    del handle
    free_gpu()

---- 5.4 ApsisNet (Bengali-specific recognizer, the recognition stage of

bbOCR — Apsis Solutions Ltd. / BRAC University / Bengali.AI, AAAI 2024).

pip install apsisnet; package/class is ApsisNet, not apsisocr.

ApsisNet is a RECOGNIZER ONLY (.infer(list_of_crops)), so it expects

pre-cropped line/word images rather than a full page. We pair it with

EasyOCR's text DETECTOR (.detect(), no recognition) to get line boxes,

crop them, sort top-to-bottom/left-to-right, then recognize each crop with

ApsisNet. Reading-order sort is a simple (y, x) heuristic, not full line

clustering - fine for single-column book pages, may mis-order multi-column

or heavily illustrated pages.

def apsisnet_load():
    import easyocr
    from apsisnet import ApsisNet
    detector = easyocr.Reader(["bn"], gpu=torch.cuda.is_available())
    recognizer = ApsisNet()
    return (detector, recognizer)
def apsisnet_unload(handle):
    del handle
    free_gpu()
def apsisnet_predict(handle, pil_img: Image.Image) -> str:
    detector, recognizer = handle
    arr = np.array(pil_img.convert("RGB"))
    horizontal_list, _free_list = detector.detect(arr)
    boxes = horizontal_list[0] if horizontal_list else []
    boxes_sorted = sorted(boxes, key=lambda b: (b[2], b[0]))  # sort by (y_min, x_min)
    crops = []
    for x_min, x_max, y_min, y_max in boxes_sorted:
        y_min, x_min = max(0, y_min), max(0, x_min)
        crop = arr[y_min:y_max, x_min:x_max]
        if crop.size > 0:
            crops.append(crop)
    if not crops:
        return ""
    texts = recognizer.infer(crops)
    return "\n".join(texts)

---- 5.5 PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 (Tier 2 - claims Bengali added in the 1.5 release,

but not in the model's own language tags and not benchmarked on Bengali by

PaddlePaddle - included so this notebook's own numbers settle the question)

API surface for paddleocr has moved fast across versions - if this errors,

check pip show paddleocr version against https://huggingface.co/PaddlePaddle/PaddleOCR-VL-1.5

def paddleocr_vl_load():
    from paddleocr import PaddleOCRVL
    try:
        return PaddleOCRVL(pipeline_version="v1.5")
    except Exception:
        import traceback; traceback.print_exc()
        raise
def paddleocr_vl_unload(handle):
    del handle
    free_gpu()
def paddleocr_vl_predict(handle, pil_img: Image.Image) -> str:
    arr = cv2.cvtColor(np.array(pil_img.convert("RGB")), cv2.COLOR_RGB2BGR)
    output = handle.predict(arr)
    res = output[0]
    if hasattr(res, "markdown"):
        return res.markdown
    if isinstance(res, dict) and "text" in res:
        return res["text"]
    return str(res)

---- 5.6 dots.ocr (rednote-hilab, 1.7B, Tier 2 - claims strong performance

across "100 languages" on an in-house benchmark; Bengali not individually

confirmed but plausible given the language count and its OmniDocBench-style

training mixture) ------------------------------------------------------------

DOTS_OCR_PROMPT = "Extract all text from this image exactly as it appears, preserving line breaks. Output only the transcription."
def dots_ocr_load():
    from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoProcessor
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
        "rednote-hilab/dots.ocr", trust_remote_code=True,
        torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda:0",
    ).eval()
    processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained("rednote-hilab/dots.ocr", trust_remote_code=True)
    return (model, processor)
def dots_ocr_unload(handle):
    del handle
    free_gpu()
def dots_ocr_predict(handle, pil_img: Image.Image) -> str:
    model, processor = handle
    messages = [{
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "image": pil_img.convert("RGB")},
            {"type": "text", "text": DOTS_OCR_PROMPT},
        ],
    }]
    text_prompt = processor.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
    inputs = processor(text=[text_prompt], images=[pil_img.convert("RGB")], return_tensors="pt").to("cuda:0")
    inputs.pop("mm_token_type_ids", None)   # <-- add this line
    with torch.no_grad():
        gen_ids = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2048, do_sample=False)
    gen_ids_trimmed = [out[len(inp):] for inp, out in zip(inputs.input_ids, gen_ids)]
    return processor.batch_decode(gen_ids_trimmed, skip_special_tokens=True, clean_up_tokenization_spaces=False)[0]

---- 5.7 baidu/Unlimited-OCR (3B, DeepSeek-OCR lineage, Tier 2 - tagged only

"multilingual", no published language list; included because it was

specifically asked about). Output embeds <|det|>type [bbox]<|/det|>

markers around each block that need stripping before scoring.

import re as _re
_DET_RE = _re.compile(r'<|det|>([^<\s]+)(?:\s*[[^]]])?\s<|/det|>(.)', _re.DOTALL)
def _unlimited_ocr_remove_det(raw: str) -> str:
    blocks, cur = [], None
    for line in raw.splitlines():
        line = line.rstrip()
        if not line:
            continue
        m = _DET_RE.match(line)
        if m:
            category, content = m.group(1).strip(), m.group(2).strip()
            if category == "image":
                continue
            if cur is not None:
                blocks.append(cur)
            cur = [content] if content else []
            continue
        if cur is None:
            cur = []
        cur.append(line)
    if cur is not None:
        blocks.append(cur)
    return "\n\n".join("\n".join(b) for b in blocks).strip()
def unlimited_ocr_load():
    from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer
    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("baidu/Unlimited-OCR", trust_remote_code=True)
    model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
        "baidu/Unlimited-OCR", trust_remote_code=True,
        use_safetensors=True, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    ).eval().to("cuda:0")
    return (model, tok)
def unlimited_ocr_unload(handle):
    del handle
    free_gpu()
def unlimited_ocr_predict(handle, pil_img: Image.Image) -> str:
    model, tok = handle
    tmp_path = "/tmp/_unlimited_ocr_page.png"
    pil_img.convert("RGB").save(tmp_path)
    out_dir = "/tmp/_unlimited_ocr_out"
    os.makedirs(out_dir, exist_ok=True)
    model.infer(
        tok, prompt="[Image: image]document parsing.", image_file=tmp_path,
        output_path=out_dir, base_size=1024, image_size=1024, crop_mode=False,
        max_length=32768, no_repeat_ngram_size=35, ngram_window=128,
        save_results=True,
    )
    # The model writes its raw output to out_dir; adjust the filename glob
    # below if a newer release changes the saved filename convention.
    result_files = sorted(Path(out_dir).glob(".md")) or sorted(Path(out_dir).glob("*.txt"))
    if not result_files:
        return ""
    raw = result_files[-1].read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    return _unlimited_ocr_remove_det(raw)

---- 5.8 GOT-OCR2.0 (general-purpose VLM OCR, 580M, Bengali not a primary

def got_ocr_load():
    from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer
    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("stepfun-ai/GOT-OCR2_0", trust_remote_code=True)
    model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
        "stepfun-ai/GOT-OCR2_0", trust_remote_code=True,
        low_cpu_mem_usage=True, device_map="cuda:0", use_safetensors=True,
    ).eval()
    return (model, tok)
def got_ocr_unload(handle):
    del handle
    free_gpu()
def got_ocr_predict(handle, pil_img: Image.Image) -> str:
    model, tok = handle
    tmp_path = "/tmp/_got_ocr_page.png"
    pil_img.convert("RGB").save(tmp_path)
    return model.chat(tok, tmp_path, ocr_type="ocr")

---- 5.9 Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, 4-bit — VLM prompted as an OCR engine ------

QWEN_PROMPT = (
    "This is a scanned page from a Bengali book. Transcribe every line of "
    "Bengali text exactly as it appears, top to bottom, preserving line "
    "breaks. Output ONLY the transcription — no commentary, no translation."
)
def qwen_vl_load():
    from transformers import Qwen2_5_VLForConditionalGeneration, AutoProcessor, BitsAndBytesConfig
    bnb_cfg = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.float16)
    model = Qwen2_5_VLForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(
        "Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct",
        quantization_config=bnb_cfg,
        device_map="cuda:0",
    ).eval()
    processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct")
    return (model, processor)
def qwen_vl_unload(handle):
    del handle
    free_gpu()
def qwen_vl_predict(handle, pil_img: Image.Image) -> str:
    model, processor = handle
    messages = [{
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "image": pil_img.convert("RGB")},
            {"type": "text", "text": QWEN_PROMPT},
        ],
    }]
    text_prompt = processor.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
    inputs = processor(text=[text_prompt], images=[pil_img.convert("RGB")], return_tensors="pt").to("cuda:0")
    with torch.no_grad():
        gen_ids = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024, do_sample=False)
    gen_ids_trimmed = [out[len(inp):] for inp, out in zip(inputs.input_ids, gen_ids)]
    out_text = processor.batch_decode(gen_ids_trimmed, skip_special_tokens=True, clean_up_tokenization_spaces=False)
    return out_text[0]

import transformers.utils.import_utils as _iu

    _iu.is_torch_fx_available = lambda: True  # torch.fx is always available on torch>=2.1

    except Exception as e:

        failed_models[tool_name] = f"load: {e}"
        continue
    for _, row in eval_sample.iterrows():
        img_path = page_img_path_for(row.book, row.page_num)

            continue
        pil_img = Image.open(img_path)
        ref = gtp.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        t0 = time.time()
        try:
            hyp = predict_fn(handle, pil_img)
        except Exception as e:
            import traceback; traceback.print_exc()   # <-- add this line
            hyp, err = "", str(e)
            hyp, err = "", str(e)
        else:
            err = None
        latency = time.time() - t0
        cer, wer = score_pair(ref, hyp)
        bakeoff_records.append({
            "tool": tool_name, "page_id": row.page_id, "book": row.book,
            "cer": cer, "wer": wer, "latency_s": latency, "error": err,
        })
    try:
        unload_fn(handle)
    except Exception:

import shutil

def surya_load():
    from surya.inference import SuryaInferenceManager
    from surya.recognition import RecognitionPredictor
    backend = os.environ.get("SURYA_INFERENCE_BACKEND", "vllm")
    if backend == "vllm" and shutil.which("docker") is None:
        raise RuntimeError(
            "surya vllm backend needs Docker, unavailable in this environment. "
            "Set SURYA_INFERENCE_BACKEND=llamacpp + install llama-server, "
            "or comment 'surya' out of MODEL_REGISTRY."

    manager = SuryaInferenceManager()
    rec = RecognitionPredictor(manager)
    return rec

def unlimited_ocr_load():
    from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer, AutoConfig
    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("baidu/Unlimited-OCR", trust_remote_code=True)
    cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("baidu/Unlimited-OCR", trust_remote_code=True)
    if getattr(cfg, "pad_token_id", None) is None:
        cfg.pad_token_id = tok.pad_token_id if tok.pad_token_id is not None else tok.eos_token_id
    model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
        "baidu/Unlimited-OCR", config=cfg, trust_remote_code=True,
        use_safetensors=True, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    ).eval().to("cuda:0")
    return (model, tok)

failed_models = {}

for tool_name, (load_fn, unload_fn, predict_fn) in MODEL_REGISTRY.items():
    print(f"\n=== {tool_name} ===")
    try:
        handle = load_fn()
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  LOAD FAILED: {e}")
        _traceback.print_exc()
        failed_models[tool_name] = f"load: {e}"
        continue

    for _, row in eval_sample.iterrows():
        img_path = page_img_path_for(row.book, row.page_num)
        gtp = gt_path_for(row.book, row.page_num)
        if not (img_path.exists() and gtp.exists()):
            continue
        pil_img = Image.open(img_path)
        ref = gtp.read_text(encoding="utf-8")

        t0 = time.time()
        try:
            hyp = predict_fn(handle, pil_img)
        except Exception as e:
            if tool_name not in _traceback_shown:
                print(f"  [{tool_name}] first page-level error (further errors on this tool are silenced):")
                _traceback.print_exc()
                _traceback_shown.add(tool_name)
            hyp, err = "", str(e)
        else:
            err = None
        latency = time.time() - t0

        cer, wer = score_pair(ref, hyp)
        bakeoff_records.append({
            "tool": tool_name, "page_id": row.page_id, "book": row.book,
            "cer": cer, "wer": wer, "latency_s": latency, "error": err,
        })

    try:
        unload_fn(handle)
    except Exception:
        pass
    del handle          # drop the outer-scope reference so free_gpu() can actually reclaim GPU memory
    free_gpu()
    n_err = sum(1 for r in bakeoff_records if r["tool"] == tool_name and r["error"])

Diagnosed deprecated cache issues and engineered targeted compatibility patches.

Good news: one of these three is a clean, well-documented fix. The other two are the same underlying problem — old trust_remote_code model code written against a transformers API that's since been torn up — but they're not equally fixable in-place.

got_ocr2 — confirmed fix, apply now

This is a known, previously-reported issue (GitHub Ucas-HaoranWei/GOT-OCR2.0#313 — same file, same line). DynamicCache.seen_tokens and .get_max_length() were both removed from transformers (v4.54 and v4.49 respectively), but GOT-OCR2's modeling_GOT.py still calls both. Since you already have the is_torch_fx_available monkeypatch pattern working, apply the same style here — one shim covers every page, no per-call patching needed:

from transformers.cache_utils import DynamicCache
if not hasattr(DynamicCache, "seen_tokens"):
    DynamicCache.seen_tokens = property(lambda self: self.get_seq_length())
if not hasattr(DynamicCache, "get_max_length"):
    DynamicCache.get_max_length = lambda self: self.get_max_cache_shape()

Put this next to your existing is_torch_fx_available patch, before the bake-off loop runs (it's a global class patch, order relative to got_ocr_load() doesn't matter as long as it runs before model.generate() is first called).

dots_ocr — worth one targeted attempt, not guaranteed

The traceback plus a matching upstream discussion make the mechanism clear: newer transformers deprecated silently building cache_position for remote-code models during the _prefill step — dots.ocr's custom prepare_inputs_for_generation still assumes it's always populated and does cache_position[0] == 0 unconditionally, so on the first call it's None and throws. The straightforward fix is to populate it yourself before calling generate(), since this is exactly the value transformers used to inject automatically:

def dots_ocr_predict(handle, pil_img: Image.Image) -> str:
    model, processor = handle
    messages = [{
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "image": pil_img.convert("RGB")},
            {"type": "text", "text": DOTS_OCR_PROMPT},
        ],
    }]
    text_prompt = processor.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
    inputs = processor(text=[text_prompt], images=[pil_img.convert("RGB")], return_tensors="pt").to("cuda:0")
    inputs.pop("mm_token_type_ids", None)
    inputs["cache_position"] = torch.arange(inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1], device="cuda:0")  # <-- add this
    with torch.no_grad():
        gen_ids = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2048, do_sample=False)
    gen_ids_trimmed = [out[len(inp):] for inp, out in zip(inputs.input_ids, gen_ids)]
    return processor.batch_decode(gen_ids_trimmed, skip_special_tokens=True, clean_up_tokenization_spaces=False)[0]

I'd call this "likely to work, not certain" — I can't verify against dots.ocr's actual source without fetching it, and if prepare_inputs_for_generation recomputes cache_position internally on each decode step rather than trusting the one you pass at prefill, this only gets you past the first token. Test it on the single-page repro you used earlier before rerunning the full 45-page loop.

unlimited_ocr — not a one-line fix; recommend dropping it or isolating it

This is the important one to be honest about. Look at the progression: your pad_token_id patch got past the first missing attribute, and the very next thing that broke was a different missing config attribute (attention_dropout) three layers deeper, inside LlamaAttention.__init__ — which the traceback shows is being reached via transformers.integrations.hub_kernels's new_init wrapper substituting in. That's not a one-off bug; it means the currently-installed transformers has a newer unified attention-class resolution system, and UnlimitedOCRConfig (a DeepSeek-V2-lineage custom config) simply doesn't define the full set of attributes that modern LlamaAttention init now expects unconditionally. Patching attention_dropout will almost certainly just surface the next missing attribute after it (rope_theta, num_key_value_heads, etc.) — this is whack-a-mole against a moving API, not a fixable bug in your wrapper.

Given the precedent you already used for ProteinBERT's OOM problem — subprocess isolation with a separately pinned environment — the same approach is the right call here rather than continuing to chase config attributes:

# One-time setup: isolated venv with an older, compatible transformers
!python -m venv /tmp/unlimited_ocr_env

I don't have a confirmed-working transformers pin for this specific model (4.46.3 is a reasonable starting guess based on when similar DeepSeek-V2-lineage custom code was commonly reported working, not a verified fact) — you'd need to test it, and possibly step down further if that version still hits a missing attribute. Given the time cost of iterating this blind, the more time-efficient call is probably to drop unlimited_ocr from the Tier 2 bake-off and note in your write-up that its custom modeling code wasn't compatible with a current transformers install without an isolated legacy environment — that's a legitimate, reportable finding rather than a debugging failure on your part.

Diagnosed tensor dimension mismatch, identified legacy implementation incompatibility.

GOT-OCR2 "size of tensor a" "must match the size of tensor b" scaled_dot_product_attention transformers

Diagnosed tensor dimension mismatch, identified legacy implementation incompatibility.

Done

The DynamicCache patch worked — you can see it got past seen_tokens/get_max_length and now fails much deeper, inside the actual attention computation. That's progress, but this new error is a different, harder class of problem.

What's happening

RuntimeError: The size of tensor a (575) must match the size of tensor b (288) at non-singleton dimension 3 is coming from inside PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention, comparing the attention mask shape against the key/value states shape. Note 575 ≈ 2×288 − 1 — that's the signature of a vision-language model where the attention_mask was built for the pre-image-expansion text sequence length, but the actual hidden states fed into attention include the spliced-in image patch embeddings, roughly doubling the effective sequence length. GOT-OCR2's custom modeling_GOT.py manually replaces token embeddings with image features inside forward(), and it looks like it isn't correspondingly expanding the attention mask it hands off to the underlying Qwen2 attention layers.

This isn't something the transformers maintainers changed arbitrarily — sdpa_attention_forward used to be more permissive about mask/key-state shape mismatches (possibly silently broadcasting or truncating), and a recent refactor made it strictly validate shapes. GOT-OCR2's custom code was written against the old, permissive behavior and never accounted for this.

One more thing worth trying — low confidence

Forcing eager attention avoids that specific strict-validation code path (sdpa_attention_forward) entirely, falling back to the older, less rigorously shape-checked attention math:

def got_ocr_load():
    from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer
    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("stepfun-ai/GOT-OCR2_0", trust_remote_code=True)
    model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
        "stepfun-ai/GOT-OCR2_0", trust_remote_code=True,
        low_cpu_mem_usage=True, device_map="cuda:0", use_safetensors=True,
        attn_implementation="eager",   # <-- add this
    ).eval()
    return (model, tok)

I'd genuinely rate this maybe 40/60 for working — it sidesteps the specific validation that's throwing, but if the underlying mask really is the wrong shape (not just validated too strictly), eager attention could still produce garbage output or a different crash further in. Test on your single-page repro before rerunning the full sample.

If that doesn't fix it — same call as unlimited_ocr

The pattern here is now the same as unlimited_ocr: a monkeypatch got you past the first layer of API drift, and what's underneath is custom model code that's structurally out of sync with the current attention/cache internals, not a one-line compatibility shim. Chasing this further means reading and patching GOT-OCR2's actual image-embedding splice logic in modeling_GOT.py, which is a real debugging project in someone else's code, not a bake-off wrapper fix.

Given you're three rounds into fixing three exploratory Tier 2 models and have working, load-bearing results from tesseract, easyocr, apsisnet_bbocr, and (pending the cache_position fix) dots_ocr, I'd suggest a line: if the eager attempt doesn't work, drop got_ocr2 from MODEL_REGISTRY and write it up alongside unlimited_ocr as "excluded — custom modeling code incompatible with current transformers without a legacy-pinned environment." That's an accurate, defensible statement for your notebook, and it stops the diminishing-returns cycle of patching increasingly deep internals in third-party trust_remote_code files you didn't write and can't fully audit without the actual source in front of you.

The problem is Qwen3-14B-AWQ is a thinking model — it's dumping its full <think>...</think> reasoning chain into the output instead of just the corrected text, so corrected is capturing rambling self-debate, not a transcription. That's exactly why WER exploded past 1.0 (the "correction" is now several paragraphs of English reasoning prose, not Bengali text at all).

Two things need to change in the prompt: explicitly kill the thinking mode (Qwen3 supports a /no_think directive in the user turn for exactly this), and make the output-only constraint much harder to ignore.

CORRECTION_PROMPT_TEMPLATE = """/no_think
You are correcting OCR output from a scanned Bengali-language book page. The OCR text below may contain misread \
characters, dropped conjuncts, merged/split words, or garbled short spans, especially where the scan is faint or \
the font is unusual.

Rules:
- Fix only clear OCR errors (misrecognized characters, obviously broken words, garbled short runs).
- Do NOT paraphrase, summarize, translate, or add content that is not implied by the OCR text itself.
- If a span is too corrupted to confidently reconstruct, leave it as-is rather than guessing new content.
- Preserve line breaks and blank lines exactly as given, including trailing blank lines.
- Do NOT reason, explain, or think out loud. Do NOT use <think> tags. Do NOT describe what you are doing.
- Your entire response must be ONLY the corrected Bengali text, starting immediately with the first character \
of the corrected page and ending immediately after the last character. No preamble, no commentary, no summary, \
no markdown, no quotation marks around the output.

OCR text:
---
{ocr_text}
---
"""

Worth knowing before you rerun: /no_think is a soft switch — it reduces the chance of a thinking block but isn't a hard guarantee across every quantized build. If Qwen3-14B still emits <think> tags with this prompt, the reliable fix is stripping them post-hoc with a regex (re.sub(r"<think>.*?</think>", "", text, flags=re.DOTALL).strip()) in qwen_batch_worker.py before scoring — I'm not adding that since you asked for just the prompt, but say the word if you want me to patch the worker too.

Yes — that's the correct fix, not the /no_think prompt hack. Qwen3's chat template accepts an enable_thinking flag, and vLLM exposes it through chat_template_kwargs on llm.chat(). That controls it at the template level rather than hoping the model obeys an in-prompt instruction.

In qwen_batch_worker.py, the correction call currently is:

outputs = llm.chat(conversations, sampling, use_tqdm=True)

Change it to:

outputs = llm.chat(
    conversations, sampling, use_tqdm=True,
    chat_template_kwargs={"enable_thinking": False},
)

Same for the per-item fallback call a few lines below it:

out = llm.chat(
    [conv], sampling, use_tqdm=False,
    chat_template_kwargs={"enable_thinking": False},
)

This only matters for text models that actually have a thinking mode (Qwen3's dense/AWQ line does; Qwen3-VL and older Qwen2.5 models generally don't use this template kwarg and will just ignore it harmlessly if passed). Since qwen_batch_worker.py is shared between OCR and correction, passing it unconditionally in both places is safe — it's a no-op for models that don't support it.

With this fix, you can drop the /no_think line from the prompt and go back to the plain version:

CORRECTION_PROMPT_TEMPLATE = """You are correcting OCR output from a scanned Bengali-language book page. The OCR text below may contain misread \
characters, dropped conjuncts, merged/split words, or garbled short spans, especially where the scan is faint or \
the font is unusual.

Rules:
- Fix only clear OCR errors (misrecognized characters, obviously broken words, garbled short runs).
- Do NOT paraphrase, summarize, translate, or add content that is not implied by the OCR text itself.
- If a span is too corrupted to confidently reconstruct, leave it as-is rather than guessing new content.
- Preserve line breaks and blank lines exactly as given, including trailing blank lines.
- Output ONLY the corrected Bengali text — no commentary, no explanation, no markdown, no quotation marks.

OCR text:
---
{ocr_text}
---
"""

One caveat worth testing rather than assuming: I'm fairly confident chat_template_kwargs is the right vLLM parameter name for this (it mirrors the same enable_thinking kwarg you already used successfully via tok.apply_chat_template(..., enable_thinking=think) in your hallucination-judge notebook), but vLLM's exact llm.chat() kwarg surface has moved across versions before in this conversation — if it raises a TypeError: unexpected keyword argument, check pip show vllm against the installed version's LLM.chat() signature; older builds sometimes call this chat_template_kwargs at the generate() level instead of chat(), or via mm_processor_kwargs misnomers in transitional releases.

Diagnosed truncation as root cause; recommended increasing token limits over prompt refinement.

Good data. Before touching the prompt, look at what's actually breaking these outputs — most of this isn't a prompt problem.

What the samples actually show

1. Truncation is the dominant failure, not bad correction. Every long page cuts off mid-word:

14B, page-152: ends at ...রূপ সার হইয়া উঠে। য — mid-sentence, missing the entire second half of the page.

14B, page-053: ends at ...কর্দম, বালুকা ও চু প — mid-word.

4B, page-152: ends at ...চর্ম মাংসের ম — mid-word.

This is max_new_tokens (1024 by default in the worker) running out mid-generation, not the model choosing to stop. Bengali is notoriously token-inefficient under BPE tokenizers — conjuncts and matras routinely split into 2-4 subword pieces each — so a page with ~300-400 Bengali words can easily need 1500-2500+ output tokens, well past your current cap. Since WER counts the entire missing tail as deleted, this alone is almost certainly why wer_delta is positive (worse) — it's punishing missing text, not wrong corrections.

2. Where a page didn't truncate, the correction is either genuinely good or a complete no-op — and the difference is model size, not prompt. Page-089 (short page, no truncation) is the clean comparison:

14B: fixed mixed Bengali/Latin digit confusion, normalized the inconsistent term (উদ্ধীমুখদস্তিত → উদ্ধমুখদন্তিত, matching the earlier occurrence on the same page), fixed the dash. Real, useful edits.

4B: output is byte-identical to input. Zero corrections attempted on a page with obvious garbling (3১77,৩, inconsistent spelling). Not a prompt-compliance failure — it just didn't find anything to fix.

That's a capability gap, not a prompt gap. No amount of prompt tuning reliably makes a 4B model catch what it structurally can't recognize as wrong. I'd hold off writing off 4B until you've fixed truncation and can see its performance on complete outputs — but expect it to keep lagging 14B on genuinely subtle errors.

3. One real prompt-fixable issue: over-correction into invented/wrong words. In page-053, স্থন্টি (the OCR's garbled version of সৃষ্টি, "creation" — a common, unambiguous word) got turned into স্থান (14B, means "place" — wrong) and স্থাস্তি (4B — not a real Bengali word at all). Both models guessed a specific reading instead of recognizing the token as ambiguous and either fixing it correctly or leaving it. This is exactly the "if too corrupted, leave as-is" rule failing to fire — it's being read as a soft suggestion rather than a hard constraint.

Fixes, in priority order

Fix truncation first — this is a generation-config change, not a prompt change. Size max_tokens per page from the input length instead of using one fixed cap for the whole batch:

def build_correction_sampling_params(manifest, base_max_new_tokens):
    from vllm import SamplingParams
    out = []
    for page in manifest:
        # Correction output length tracks input length; Bengali's poor token
        # efficiency (multiple subword pieces per conjunct) means a cap sized
        # for English text truncates mid-page. This multiplier is a rough
        # starting point - if [AFTER] samples still cut off mid-word, raise it.
        input_len_chars = len(page.get("hyp_text", ""))
        est_tokens = int(input_len_chars * 1.3) + 150
        max_tokens = max(base_max_new_tokens, min(est_tokens, 4096))
        out.append(SamplingParams(temperature=0, max_tokens=max_tokens, repetition_penalty=1.05))
    return out

Then pass the list instead of a single SamplingParams to llm.chat(conversations, sampling_list, use_tqdm=True, chat_template_kwargs={"enable_thinking": False}). I believe llm.chat() accepts a per-conversation list matching generate()'s pattern, but verify this against your installed vLLM version — if it rejects a list, the fallback is bumping the single shared value to something generously large (e.g. max_new_tokens=3072) instead.

Then, yes, add a semantic-plausibility nudge — but narrowly, to stop invented words rather than to make the model "think harder":

CORRECTION_PROMPT_TEMPLATE = """You are correcting OCR output from a scanned Bengali-language book page. The OCR text below may contain misread \
characters, dropped conjuncts, merged/split words, or garbled short spans, especially where the scan is faint or \
the font is unusual.

Rules:
- Fix only clear OCR errors (misrecognized characters, obviously broken words, garbled short runs).
- Do NOT paraphrase, summarize, translate, or add content that is not implied by the OCR text itself.
- Before applying a fix, check that the corrected word is a real, contextually sensible Bengali word given the \
surrounding sentence. If two or more different real words could plausibly fit a garbled span, or if you cannot \
identify a specific real word that fits, leave the span exactly as it appears in the OCR text rather than guessing.
- Preserve line breaks and blank lines exactly as given, including trailing blank lines.
- Output ONLY the corrected Bengali text — no commentary, no explanation, no markdown, no quotation marks.

OCR text:
---
{ocr_text}
---
"""

The load-bearing addition is the third rule — it converts "leave as-is if uncertain" from a vague fallback into a concrete check (does a specific real word fit, or not) before the model commits to an edit. I'd stop there rather than pushing further into "consider semantics broadly" — a stronger semantic nudge risks the opposite failure mode, where the model starts "fixing" things that are already correct because it decided a different word would fit the sentence better, which is a much harder error to catch by inspection than an untouched garbled span.

Re-run with the token-budget fix alone first, since it's likely responsible for most of the current wer_delta damage — then decide whether the semantic-plausibility rule is still needed once truncation stops inflating every long page's WER.

"""Stage 1 — deskew / denoise / binarize / augment"""
from __future__ import annotations
from ..contracts import *  # noqa
from pathlib import Path

import cv2
import numpy as np

IMAGE_EXTS = {".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".tif", ".tiff"}

def _cfg_get(cfg: dict, key: str, default):
    return cfg.get("ingest", {}).get(key, default)

def _page_stats(image_path: Path, min_blob_area: int) -> dict:
    img = cv2.imread(str(image_path), cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
    if img is None:
        raise ValueError(f"OpenCV could not read {image_path}")
    _, binary = cv2.threshold(img, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY_INV + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)
    kernel = np.ones((2, 2), np.uint8)
    cleaned = cv2.morphologyEx(binary, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, kernel)
    _num_labels, _labels, stats, _centroids = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(cleaned, connectivity=8)
    areas = stats[1:, cv2.CC_STAT_AREA]
    real_blobs = areas[areas >= min_blob_area]
    total_pixels = img.shape[0] * img.shape[1]
    ink_ratio = float(real_blobs.sum()) / total_pixels if total_pixels else 0.0
    return {"blob_count": int(len(real_blobs)), "ink_ratio": ink_ratio}

def _is_blank(stats: dict, min_blob_count: int, ink_ratio_threshold: float) -> bool:
    return stats["blob_count"] < min_blob_count or stats["ink_ratio"] < ink_ratio_threshold

def run(pages: list[Page], cfg: dict) -> list[Page]:
    """Filter likely-blank page-images; splitting/rendering is handled by loader.load_pages()."""
    data_root = Path(_cfg_get(cfg, "data_root", "data"))
    blank_root = data_root / _cfg_get(cfg, "blank_dir", "blank")

    min_blob_area = int(_cfg_get(cfg, "min_blob_area", 15))
    ink_ratio_threshold = float(_cfg_get(cfg, "ink_ratio_threshold", 0.002))
    min_blob_count = int(_cfg_get(cfg, "min_blob_count", 3))

    blank_root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    processed: list[Page] = []
    for page in pages:
        doc_id = page.doc_id
        image_path = Path(page.image_path)
        stats = _page_stats(image_path, min_blob_area=min_blob_area)
        if _is_blank(stats, min_blob_count=min_blob_count, ink_ratio_threshold=ink_ratio_threshold):
            dest_dir = blank_root / doc_id
            dest_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            dest_path = dest_dir / image_path.name
            image_path.replace(dest_path)
            continue

        processed.append(page)

    return processed

Good catch — comparing the two implementations, three concrete things differ, and each one biases toward over-flagging real content as blank:

What's wrong with the "current" (notebook) version

Notebook version (< 2% foreground density)
Your run() version
Threshold
< 0.02 (2%)
< 0.002 (0.2%) — 10x stricter
Noise handling
None — raw Otsu binary counted directly
cv2.MORPH_OPEN (2×2 kernel) before counting, to erase speckle
What gets counted
Every foreground pixel, including 1–2px scan noise
Only pixels belonging to blobs >= min_blob_area (15px) — noise blobs are dropped entirely
Second signal
None
blob_count < 3 as an OR condition — catches "almost nothing there" pages even if ink_ratio is borderline

The overestimation is driven almost entirely by the threshold gap, not the noise handling. A 2% floor is too high for real 1930s typesetting — a chapter-divider page, a page with one short heading and generous margins, or a page whose only content is a page number and a single line, can easily sit at 0.5–1.5% ink coverage. All of those get wrongly swept into "blank" under the 2% rule, even though they're genuine content pages.

The missing min_blob_area filter cuts the other way (it would tend to undercount blanks, since noise inflates density and keeps truly-blank pages above threshold) — so it's not the culprit, but it's still worth adding for a stable metric, and the blob_count check is a genuinely useful second signal your notebook version lacks entirely.

What to change

Drop the threshold from 0.02 → 0.002 (or better: don't hardcode it in the EDA — import the actual value from the pipeline's ingest config so the two never drift apart).

Add the MORPH_OPEN denoise step before thresholding.

Filter connected components by min_blob_area before summing ink pixels, rather than counting every raw foreground pixel.

Add blob_count < min_blob_count as an OR condition alongside the ink-ratio check.

I'll update the EDA notebook's Section 1 to call the exact same logic as your run() function (not a re-derived approximation), so the EDA's blank-page pass and the actual ingest stage can never silently disagree.

Two separate issues here — let me take them one at a time.

Why PaddleOCR is all NaN

Every value being NaN (not just high) means every single call to ocr_paddleocr() is throwing an exception, which the bake-off's try/except silently swallows into cer, wer = np.nan, np.nan. The likely culprits, in order of probability:

API mismatch — I pinned paddleocr>=2.7,<3.0, but PaddleOCR 3.x changed the API significantly (use_angle_cls → use_textline_orientation, .ocr(..., cls=True) → .predict(...), and the return shape changed from nested lists to result objects with .rec_texts). If your installed version doesn't match the pin, line[1][0] in my parsing code will raise on every call.

First-run model download — PaddleOCR pulls detection/recognition/orientation model weights from PaddlePaddle's servers on first use. If that's blocked (offline Kaggle session, firewall, etc.), every call fails at init.

lang="bn" model availability — worth confirming this actually resolves to a real model bundle in your installed version rather than silently failing.

The fix isn't guessing — it's making the failure visible. Right now the notebook hides the actual exception message. Let me add a diagnostic cell and print real errors instead of swallowing them.

Markdown symbols — yes, this is a real gap

You're right to suspect this. Gemini's transcriptions often come back with light Markdown structure — **bold** for headings, #/## for section titles, -/• bullets, | table pipes, sometimes stray backticks — even when asked for plain transcription. OCR engines (Tesseract/EasyOCR/PaddleOCR) never emit any of that; they output raw glyphs only. So every *, #, -, | sitting in the GT reference is an automatic edit-distance penalty against the hypothesis, inflating CER/WER for reasons that have nothing to do with OCR quality.

def ocr_paddleocr(pil_img):
    """PaddleOCR's return shape changed between 2.x (nested list: [[[box, (text, score)], ...]])
    and 3.x (list of result objects with .rec_texts / ["rec_texts"]). Handle both rather than
    assuming one -- a shape mismatch here is the most common reason this tool comes back
    all-NaN in the bake-off (silent exception, not a real OCR failure)."""
    reader = get_paddle_reader()
    img_arr = np.array(pil_img)

    # Try the modern .predict() interface first (PaddleOCR >=3.0)
    if hasattr(reader, "predict"):
        result = reader.predict(img_arr)
        lines = []
        for res in (result or []):
            texts = res.get("rec_texts") if isinstance(res, dict) else getattr(res, "rec_texts", None)
            if texts:
                lines.extend(texts)
        if lines:
            return "\n".join(lines)

    # Fall back to the legacy .ocr() interface (PaddleOCR 2.x)
    result = reader.ocr(img_arr, cls=True)
    lines = []
    for block in (result or []):
        for line in (block or []):
            # line == [box, (text, score)]
            lines.append(line[1][0])
    return "\n".join(lines)

2. normalize_for_scoring() — replace this function (used in both the bake-off and preprocessing-sweep cells):

def normalize_for_scoring(text):
    """NFC-normalize, strip Markdown structure, and collapse whitespace so CER/WER isn't
    inflated by formatting noise. Gemini GT frequently comes back with light Markdown
    (headings, bullets, bold, table pipes) that no OCR engine ever emits -- every one of
    those stray symbols is a free edit-distance penalty against the hypothesis, so they
    must be stripped from BOTH ref and hyp before scoring, not just whitespace-collapsed."""
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text)

    # Fenced code blocks -> drop entirely (Gemini sometimes wraps tables/lists in ``` )
    text = re.sub(r"```.*?```", " ", text, flags=re.DOTALL)
    # Inline code spans -> keep content, drop backticks
    text = re.sub(r"`([^`]*)`", r"\1", text)
    # ATX headings: leading #'s
    text = re.sub(r"(?m)^\s{0,3}#{1,6}\s*", "", text)
    # Bold / italic / strikethrough markers (Bengali script never uses these ASCII symbols)
    text = re.sub(r"\*\*\*|\*\*|\*|__|~~", "", text)
    # Bullet list markers at line start (-, *, +, • )
    text = re.sub(r"(?m)^\s*[-*+•]\s+", "", text)
    # Numbered list markers at line start ("1. ", "12) ")
    text = re.sub(r"(?m)^\s*\d+[.)]\s+", "", text)
    # Blockquote markers
    text = re.sub(r"(?m)^\s*>\s?", "", text)
    # Horizontal rules ( ---, ***, === on their own line )
    text = re.sub(r"(?m)^\s*([-*=_])\1{2,}\s*$", "", text)
    # Table pipes -> space (keep cell content, drop the delimiter itself)
    text = text.replace("|", " ")
    # Markdown links / images: [text](url) or ![alt](url) -> keep just the text
    text = re.sub(r"!?\[([^\]]*)\]\([^)]*\)", r"\1", text)

    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()
    return text

# --- Diagnostic: run each available tool ONCE on a single page, with the exception
# surfaced in full, before the big loop. The bake-off's try/except silently turns any
# failure into NaN, which is exactly why "all NaN for one tool" gives no clue on its own --
# this cell is where you find out *why*, instead of guessing.
import traceback

_diag_img = Image.open(page_img_path_for(eval_sample.iloc[0].book, eval_sample.iloc[0].page_num))

for tool_name, ocr_fn in OCR_FUNCS.items():
    if not TOOLS_AVAILABLE.get(tool_name):
        print(f"[{tool_name}] not installed, skipped")
        continue
    try:
        out = ocr_fn(_diag_img)
        print(f"[{tool_name}] OK -- {len(out)} chars, e.g. {out[:60]!r}")
    except Exception:
        print(f"[{tool_name}] FAILED -- full traceback below:")
        traceback.print_exc()
    print("-" * 60)

4. Main bake-off loop cell — replace with this (adds first-failure printing + an all-NaN summary at the end):

bakeoff_records = []
_printed_error_for = set()  # print only the FIRST failure per tool -- avoids flooding
                             # the log with one traceback per page while still surfacing
                             # the actual cause instead of a silent all-NaN column.

for _, row in tqdm(eval_sample.iterrows(), total=len(eval_sample), desc="OCR bake-off"):
    img_path = page_img_path_for(row.book, row.page_num)
    gtp = gt_path_for(row.book, row.page_num)
    if not (img_path.exists() and gtp.exists()):
        continue
    pil_img = Image.open(img_path)
    ref = normalize_for_scoring(gtp.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    if not ref:
        continue

    for tool_name, ocr_fn in OCR_FUNCS.items():
        if not TOOLS_AVAILABLE.get(tool_name):
            continue
        try:
            hyp = normalize_for_scoring(ocr_fn(pil_img))
            cer = jiwer.cer(ref, hyp) if hyp else 1.0
            wer = jiwer.wer(ref, hyp) if hyp else 1.0
        except Exception as e:
            cer, wer, hyp = np.nan, np.nan, f"[ERROR: {e}]"
            if tool_name not in _printed_error_for:
                print(f"\n[{tool_name}] first failure on {row.page_id}: {e!r}")
                _printed_error_for.add(tool_name)
        bakeoff_records.append({
            "page_id": row.page_id, "book": row.book, "tool": tool_name,
            "cer": cer, "wer": wer, "hyp_len": len(hyp) if isinstance(hyp, str) else 0,
        })

bakeoff_df = pd.DataFrame(bakeoff_records)
if not bakeoff_df.empty:
    fail_rate = bakeoff_df.groupby("tool")["cer"].apply(lambda s: s.isna().mean())
    fully_failed = fail_rate[fail_rate == 1.0]
    if not fully_failed.empty:
        print(f"\nTool(s) that failed on EVERY page (all-NaN): {list(fully_failed.index)}")
        print("See the diagnostic cell above for the actual exception, or re-run it after fixing.")

That traceback tells you exactly what's going on — this isn't a bug in the notebook, it's a real capability gap in your installed PaddleOCR:

This version of PaddleOCR does not support Bengali at all. PaddleOCR 3.x consolidated its language list into broad script families (latin, arabic, cyrillic, devanagari, plus a few explicit languages like Tamil/Telugu/Kannada) and dropped the explicit bn code that 2.x had. Bengali script isn't Devanagari, so it doesn't fall under any supported family here — it's simply not covered by this release, independent of anything in your pipeline.

Two things worth checking before you decide what to do:

Confirm what's actually installed — your pyproject.toml pins paddleocr>=2.7,<3.0, but this traceback's error shape matches the 3.x API. Run uv pip show paddleocr and check the version. If it's 3.x despite the <3.0 pin, that means the lockfile/sync didn't actually pick up your constraint (possibly leftover from before the ocr extra was moved into [project.optional-dependencies] — worth re-running uv lock && uv sync --extra ocr from a clean venv to be sure).

If downgrading to 2.x, older PaddleOCR did support lang="bn" via its multilingual PP-OCRv3 recognition model — that would actually fix this. If you want to stay on 3.x, Bengali isn't available in it at all right now, and no code change on our end can work around that.

Given the uncertainty, here's the pragmatic fix: detect this specific failure at startup and mark PaddleOCR unavailable with a clear message, instead of crashing the diagnostic/bake-off cells every run.

This does construct the PaddleOCR(lang="bn") object once as a probe — if your version supports it, that instance gets thrown away and get_paddle_reader() builds a fresh one lazily as before (harmless, just a few extra seconds at startup). 1. Test the exact interpreter directly, bypassing python on PATH

.venv/bin/python -c "import cv2; print(cv2.__file__); print(cv2.__version__)"

If this fails too, the problem is inside the venv itself (a broken/partial install despite what pip list shows) — skip to step 4. If this succeeds, the problem is that python scripts/run_ingest.py isn't actually running through .venv/bin/python — go to step 2.

2. Run the script with the explicit interpreter path

.venv/bin/python scripts/run_ingest.py

If this works, your shell's python command was silently resolving elsewhere. Check:

3. Check for a local file/folder shadowing cv2

This is a classic gotcha: when you run python scripts/run_ingest.py, Python puts scripts/ at the front of sys.path. If anything named cv2.py or a cv2/ directory exists anywhere on that path (most likely in scripts/ or your project root), it shadows the real installed package before Python ever reaches site-packages.

should print arm64 on Apple Silicon — if it prints x86_64, your venv's Python itself is running under Rosetta, and you'd want to confirm uv python list / how .venv was created isn't pulling an Intel build.

"""Stage 1 — load scanned page-images"""
from __future__ import annotations
from ..contracts import *  # noqa
from ..data import validate
from ..data import snapshot
from pathlib import Path
from pdf2image import convert_from_path

IMAGE_EXTS = {".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".tif", ".tiff"}

def _cfg_get(cfg: dict, key: str, default):
    return cfg.get("ingest", {}).get(key, default)

def _render_pdfs_to_pages(raw_root: Path, pages_root: Path, dpi: int) -> None:
    pages_root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for pdf_path in sorted(raw_root.glob("*.pdf")):
        doc_id = pdf_path.stem
        out_dir = pages_root / doc_id
        out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

        if any(out_dir.glob("*.png")):
            continue

        images = convert_from_path(str(pdf_path), dpi=dpi)
        for i, img in enumerate(images, start=1):
            out_path = out_dir / f"page-{i:03d}.png"
            if not out_path.exists():
                img.save(out_path, "PNG")

def _iter_pages(pages_root: Path) -> list[Page]:
    pages: list[Page] = []
    if not pages_root.exists():
        return pages
    for doc_dir in sorted(p for p in pages_root.iterdir() if p.is_dir()):
        for image_path in sorted(p for p in doc_dir.rglob("*") if p.suffix.lower() in IMAGE_EXTS):
            page_id = f"{doc_dir.name}:{image_path.stem}"
            pages.append(Page(id=page_id, image_path=str(image_path), doc_id=doc_dir.name))
    return pages

def load_pages(cfg: dict) -> list[Page]:
    """Read PDFs from data/raw, render to data/pages, then return page-image records."""
    data_root = Path(_cfg_get(cfg, "data_root", "data"))
    raw_root = data_root / _cfg_get(cfg, "raw_dir", "raw")
    pages_root = data_root / _cfg_get(cfg, "pages_dir", "pages")
    dpi = int(_cfg_get(cfg, "render_dpi", 150))

    _render_pdfs_to_pages(raw_root, pages_root, dpi)
    pages = _iter_pages(pages_root)
    if not pages:
        raise ValueError(f"No page images found under {pages_root}. Ensure PDFs exist in {raw_root}.")
    
    validate(pages)
    snapshot(data_root) 
    
    return pages

Analyzed resolution loss, compared extraction versus rendering, identified duplicate pages via object IDs.

Analyzed resolution loss, compared extraction versus rendering, identified duplicate pages via object IDs.

Done

Good catch running pdfimages -list — this answers the question directly, and the answer is: yes, you're discarding real information, and you should extract, not render.

What "stencil" vs "image" means here

Both are the same kind of scanned content — a single full-page bitonal (black/white) bitmap per page, compressed with a fax-style codec (CCITT Group 4 or JBIG2). The difference is just which PDF object type wraps it:

image (Krishi-Bigyan, Krishi-Darpan): a normal raster image object, DeviceGray, 1 bit per pixel. The pixel values themselves encode black/white directly.

stencil (Bharater-Krishi-Babyasthar-Parichay): a PDF ImageMask — a 1-bit boolean matte with no color of its own. Wherever the mask bit is "on," the PDF paints it with whatever fill color is active at that point (virtually always black, for a scanned page). It's a common trick for compressing bitonal scans slightly differently, but visually and informationally it's the same thing: a black-on-white page scan.

Neither is lossy or special — they're both just 1-bit fax-compressed scans, one wrapped as a plain image, one wrapped as a paint mask.

The real issue: native resolution vs. your render DPI

pdfimages -list reports the actual embedded resolution:

Book
Native resolution
Pixel dimensions
Bharater-Krishi...
~435 ppi
3090 × 4790
Krishi-Bigyan
600 ppi
2990 × 4690
Krishi-Darpan
600 ppi
2274 × 3651

Your loader's default is render_dpi = 150. Rendering at 150 (or even 300) means pdftoppm/pdf2image is downsampling an already-decoded 435–600 ppi bitonal scan down to a fraction of its native resolution, and — worse — doing it with anti-aliasing, which turns crisp black/white Bengali strokes and matras into blurred gray edges before your pipeline ever sees them. For a script with fine conjuncts and diacritics, that's exactly the detail you can't afford to throw away. So: yes, rendering at 300 is still discarding real information, since native is 435–600.

Render or extract? Extract.

Since each page is literally one embedded scanned image with nothing else on it (no separate text layer, no vector overlays — pdfimages -list shows exactly one image object per page), there's no reason to rasterize the PDF through Poppler's rendering pipeline at all. pdfimages extracts the original embedded bitmap byte-for-byte at full native resolution, with no resampling, no anti-aliasing, and it's faster (no rasterization pass, just stream decoding).

Bonus finding from your -list output

Look at the object ID column: Book 1 pages 1, 2, 3, 5 all reference the same object ID (5). Book 3 pages 1, 2, 3, 5 all reference object ID 4. That means those pages share the literal same embedded image bytes — they're not just visually similar, they're byte-identical. That's a much stronger, zero-compute blank-page signal than your density heuristic, and worth cross-checking against what your blank-page filter actually flagged.

Updated loader

"""Stage 1 — load scanned page-images"""
from __future__ import annotations
from ..contracts import *  # noqa
from ..data import validate
from ..data import snapshot
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import shutil
import hashlib

IMAGE_EXTS = {".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".tif", ".tiff"}

def _cfg_get(cfg: dict, key: str, default):
    return cfg.get("ingest", {}).get(key, default)

def _extract_pdf_images(raw_root: Path, pages_root: Path) -> None:
    """Extract embedded page scans at native resolution via `pdfimages`, instead of
    re-rasterizing the PDF at a fixed DPI. These corpora are single scanned-image-per-page
    PDFs (confirmed via `pdfimages -list`: one image object per page, 435-600 native ppi) --
    rendering through pdftoppm at a lower DPI than the source only throws away resolution
    and introduces anti-aliasing blur that wasn't in the original scan.
    """
    if shutil.which("pdfimages") is None:
        raise RuntimeError(
            "pdfimages not found on PATH. It ships with poppler-utils, the same package "
            "pdf2image depends on -- `brew install poppler` (macOS) should provide it."
        )

    pages_root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for pdf_path in sorted(raw_root.glob("*.pdf")):
        doc_id = pdf_path.stem
        out_dir = pages_root / doc_id
        out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

        if any(out_dir.glob("*.png")):
            continue

        # pdfimages numbers output files by extraction order, which matches page order
        # for these single-image-per-page PDFs. Extract to a temp prefix, then rename to
        # the page-NNN.png convention the rest of the pipeline expects.
        prefix = out_dir / "_extract"
        subprocess.run(
            ["pdfimages", "-png", str(pdf_path), str(prefix)],
            check=True, capture_output=True,
        )

        extracted = sorted(out_dir.glob("_extract-*.png"))
        if not extracted:
            raise ValueError(f"pdfimages extracted no images from {pdf_path}")

        seen_hashes: dict[str, str] = {}
        for i, src in enumerate(extracted, start=1):
            dest = out_dir / f"page-{i:03d}.png"
            src.rename(dest)
            # Cheap duplicate-page detector: pages sharing the same underlying scan
            # (e.g. reused blank/endpaper templates) will hash identically.
            digest = hashlib.md5(dest.read_bytes()).hexdigest()
            if digest in seen_hashes:
                print(f"[{doc_id}] {dest.name} is byte-identical to {seen_hashes[digest]} "
                      f"(likely a duplicated blank/template page)")
            seen_hashes[digest] = dest.name

def _iter_pages(pages_root: Path) -> list[Page]:
    pages: list[Page] = []
    if not pages_root.exists():
        return pages
    for doc_dir in sorted(p for p in pages_root.iterdir() if p.is_dir()):
        for image_path in sorted(p for p in doc_dir.rglob("*") if p.suffix.lower() in IMAGE_EXTS):
            page_id = f"{doc_dir.name}:{image_path.stem}"
            pages.append(Page(id=page_id, image_path=str(image_path), doc_id=doc_dir.name))
    return pages

def load_pages(cfg: dict) -> list[Page]:
    """Read PDFs from data/raw, extract native-resolution page scans to data/pages, then
    return page-image records."""
    data_root = Path(_cfg_get(cfg, "data_root", "data"))
    raw_root = data_root / _cfg_get(cfg, "raw_dir", "raw")
    pages_root = data_root / _cfg_get(cfg, "pages_dir", "pages")

    _extract_pdf_images(raw_root, pages_root)
    pages = _iter_pages(pages_root)
    if not pages:
        raise ValueError(f"No page images found under {pages_root}. Ensure PDFs exist in {raw_root}.")

    validate(pages)
    snapshot(data_root)

    return pages

Note render_dpi is no longer used — extraction ignores it entirely since there's no rasterization step. If you still want a pdf2image-based fallback for some future PDF that actually has vector content (not just embedded scans), keep the old function around under a different name and branch on it, but for this corpus extraction is strictly better.

One thing worth verifying after switching

Run pdfimages -list once more per book and compare page counts against len(extracted) in the new loader — for these three PDFs it should line up 1:1, but it's worth a sanity assert (e.g. compare against pypdf.PdfReader(pdf_path).pages count) in case any page ever has zero or multiple embedded images.

Analyzed DPI resolution preservation and engineered robust rendering strategy.

What "stencil" vs "image" actually means here

Both are 1-bit-per-pixel (bpc 1) bilevel rasters — the only difference is how the PDF stores color:

image (Krishi-Bigyan, Krishi-Darpan): a real DeviceGray XObject. Each pixel is either black or white, stored directly.

stencil (Bharater-Krishi-Babyasthar-Parichay): an ImageMask — a 1-bit mask with no color of its own. The content stream paints it with whatever fill color is active (almost always black), so it renders as black-on-white text just the same. It's not "less information," just a different encoding trick (common output of scan-to-PDF tools using CCITT Group 4).

ccitt and jbig2 are both lossless bilevel compression schemes built for exactly this (fax/scan text). So nothing has been thrown away yet at the PDF-storage level — the loss risk is entirely in your rendering step.

Are you discarding information at 300 DPI? Yes — for two of your three corpora.

The x-ppi/y-ppi columns from pdfimages -list aren't arbitrary metadata — they're the effective resolution the image was scanned/embedded at, relative to the PDF page box. That's your ground truth for "native resolution." Pulling the max per corpus:

Corpus
Native resolution
Physical page size (computed)
Krishi-Bigyan
600 ppi
2990/600 × 4690/600 = 4.98" × 7.82"
Krishi-Darpan
600 ppi
2274/600 × 3651/600 = 3.79" × 6.09"
Bharater-Krishi-Babyasthar-Parichay
435 ppi (one outlier page at 450)
3090/435 × 4790/435 = 7.10" × 11.01"

Rendering at 150 DPI (your current default) or 300 DPI downsamples the first two corpora by 4x / 2x respectively — poppler will resample and antialias, which for bilevel scanned text means thin strokes (Bengali matras, conjunct joins, reph marks) get blurred or merged. That's exactly the kind of degradation that quietly tanks OCR/TrOCR accuracy without you noticing until Stage 4+ output looks "off" for no obvious reason. 300 DPI is roughly fine for the third corpus (435 ppi) but still slightly under.

Bottom line: render, don't guess a DPI — detect the native resolution per PDF and render at or above it.

Render vs. extract?

Stick with rendering (pdf2image/poppler), not raw pdfimages extraction, for two reasons:

Poppler correctly composites stencil masks into a proper black-on-white raster; a raw mask extraction gives you a colorless 1-bit mask you'd have to composite yourself.

Poppler respects any page /Rotate flag; pdfimages extraction does not — you'd risk sideways pages silently.

Just fix the DPI to match the source instead of using a fixed 150/300.

One more landmine in your current code

if any(out_dir.glob("*.png")):
    continue

This caches renders forever — if you change the DPI logic and rerun, it'll silently keep the old low-res PNGs because some PNG exists. I've replaced this with a small metadata marker that re-renders whenever the target DPI or source PDF changes.

Also worth flagging (not fixed below, just noting): several pages share the same object ID (e.g. object 5 reused across pages 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 in Bharater-Krishi at ~600B each) — these are near-identical blank/cover pages. Not a rendering bug, but Stage 2+ might want to know which pages are duplicates so you don't burn OCR compute on blank leaves. I left a hook for this (is_likely_blank) but didn't force any behavior — that's a judgment call for your pipeline.

"""Stage 1 — deskew / denoise / binarize / augment"""
from __future__ import annotations
from ..contracts import *  # noqa
from pathlib import Path

import cv2
import numpy as np

IMAGE_EXTS = {".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".tif", ".tiff"}

def _cfg_get(cfg: dict, key: str, default):
    return cfg.get("ingest", {}).get(key, default)

def _page_stats(image_path: Path, min_blob_area: int) -> dict:
    img = cv2.imread(str(image_path), cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
    if img is None:
        raise ValueError(f"OpenCV could not read {image_path}")
    _, binary = cv2.threshold(img, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY_INV + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)
    kernel = np.ones((2, 2), np.uint8)
    cleaned = cv2.morphologyEx(binary, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, kernel)
    _num_labels, _labels, stats, _centroids = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(cleaned, connectivity=8)
    areas = stats[1:, cv2.CC_STAT_AREA]
    real_blobs = areas[areas >= min_blob_area]
    total_pixels = img.shape[0] * img.shape[1]
    ink_ratio = float(real_blobs.sum()) / total_pixels if total_pixels else 0.0
    return {"blob_count": int(len(real_blobs)), "ink_ratio": ink_ratio}

def _is_blank(stats: dict, min_blob_count: int, ink_ratio_threshold: float) -> bool:
    return stats["blob_count"] < min_blob_count or stats["ink_ratio"] < ink_ratio_threshold

def run(pages: list[Page], cfg: dict) -> list[Page]:
    """Filter likely-blank page-images; splitting/rendering is handled by loader.load_pages()."""
    data_root = Path(_cfg_get(cfg, "data_root", "data"))
    blank_root = data_root / _cfg_get(cfg, "blank_dir", "blank")

    min_blob_area = int(_cfg_get(cfg, "min_blob_area", 15))
    ink_ratio_threshold = float(_cfg_get(cfg, "ink_ratio_threshold", 0.002))
    min_blob_count = int(_cfg_get(cfg, "min_blob_count", 3))

    blank_root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    processed: list[Page] = []
    for page in pages:
        doc_id = page.doc_id
        image_path = Path(page.image_path)
        stats = _page_stats(image_path, min_blob_area=min_blob_area)
        if _is_blank(stats, min_blob_count=min_blob_count, ink_ratio_threshold=ink_ratio_threshold):
            dest_dir = blank_root / doc_id
            dest_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            dest_path = dest_dir / image_path.name
            image_path.replace(dest_path)
            continue

        processed.append(page)

    return processed

Dependencies

Nothing new to add to pyproject.toml — everything the loader uses (subprocess, shutil, json, pathlib) is stdlib, and pdf2image is already listed.

The one thing to be aware of: I call the pdfimages binary via subprocess, not a Python package. It's part of poppler-utils — the same system package that ships pdftoppm, which pdf2image already depends on to run at all. Since your original loader was already working, poppler is already installed on your machine, and pdfimages should already be sitting right next to pdftoppm in that same install. Nothing to add — just flagging it's a system binary, not a pip dependency, so it won't show up in pyproject.toml regardless.

I also had a leftover unused import re in the loader from an earlier draft — removed it.

Is the loader accurate?

Yes — I re-verified the column parsing against your actual pasted list, not just my earlier sample:

53    52 stencil  3337  4945  -       1   1  ccitt  no       273  0   450   450 29.6K 1.5%

splits into 16 tokens, parts[12]=450, parts[13]=450 → correctly picked up as the resolution outlier for Bharater-Krishi. Confirmed against Krishi-Darpan (parts[12]=600) and Krishi-Bigyan (parts[12]=600) rows too. The parts[0].isdigit() guard correctly skips the header and ---- separator lines. So the DPI detection logic checks out against your real data.

preprocess.py — one real inconsistency, and it's caused by my change

The blank-page thresholds are tuned for a fixed low DPI, but pages now arrive at variable native DPI (600 vs 450).

min_blob_area=15 is an absolute pixel count, and your (2,2) opening kernel is an absolute pixel size. Blob area scales with DPI², so a scanner-noise speck that was correctly filtered out (<15px) at 150 DPI is now ~16x larger in pixel area at 600 DPI and ~9x larger at 450 DPI — it'll clear the area threshold and get counted as a real "blob." Net effect: genuinely blank pages are now more likely to be misclassified as non-blank, and worse, the misclassification rate differs by corpus (16x drift for Bigyan/Darpan vs 9x for Bharater-Krishi) since they render at different native DPIs. Any threshold you tune by eye on one corpus won't transfer to the other.

Fix: compute blank-page stats on a resolution-normalized downsampled copy (fixed max dimension, independent of native render DPI), while leaving the actual OCR input untouched at full native resolution. This also cuts your connectedComponentsWithStats cost, which was going to get noticeably heavier now that pages are 3000×4700+ instead of ~1200×1800.

Second issue — destructive, non-idempotent move:

image_path.replace(dest_path)

This moves the file out of data/pages/doc_id/. Combined with my loader's caching (which only checks "does some PNG exist"), that means: once a page is filed away as blank, if you ever loosen/tighten ink_ratio_threshold and rerun Stage 2, the page is already gone from pages_root — you can't reclassify it without deleting _render_meta.json and forcing a full, expensive re-render of the whole document. Fix: copy instead of move, so pages_root always stays a complete, re-classifiable snapshot; blank_dir becomes an inspection copy, not the only remaining copy.

Minor: the module docstring still says "deskew / denoise / binarize / augment" but the function only filters blanks — worth updating so future-you isn't confused about what's actually implemented yet.
