Was facing the following error.

Assistant:

8/11/2026 13:55:22

Diagnosed GPU cache incompatibility and parsed data loading logic.

Diagnosed GPU cache incompatibility and parsed data loading logic.

Done

Root cause

This is a known bug: torch.nn.DataParallel (which Trainer uses automatically on multi-GPU when you're not using proper distributed training) breaks with the newer transformers Cache/EncoderDecoderCache classes. When use_cache=False per-replica, past_key_values returns as None on each GPU replica, and PyTorch's DataParallel.gather() tries to reconstruct a merged Cache object from those Nones across replicas — which crashes in Cache.__init__ trying to read .dtype off None.

This isn't something you can fix by tweaking use_cache further — it's fundamentally incompatible with naive DataParallel in current transformers versions. The practical fix on Kaggle's 2×T4 notebook (without setting up full accelerate/DDP via notebook_launcher, which is a lot of extra complexity for two T4s) is to restrict training to a single GPU.

Fix: force single-GPU

Add this as the very first cell in the notebook, before any import torch or CUDA-touching import:

import os
os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = "0"   # avoid DataParallel + Cache bug on multi-GPU

If you've already run cells and CUDA is initialized, you'll need to restart the kernel for this to take effect — CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES only works before CUDA context creation.

Since you lose the second GPU, bump per_device_train_batch_size up if VRAM allows, and adjust gradient_accumulation_steps to hit a similar effective batch size as before (previously 8×2×2=32 effective on 2 GPUs; single-GPU with batch=8, accum=4 gets you back to 32).

import os
import glob
import re
import pandas as pd

ALIGNED_LINES_DIR = os.path.join(LINES_DIR, "aligned_doctr")

# Filenames from build_aligned_line_dataset:
#   {page_id}_seg{seg_idx:03d}_gt{gt_idx:03d}.png
# Only accepted (CER <= threshold) pairs were ever written to disk,
# so every file found here is already a validated alignment -- no
# need to re-check CER or re-parse the log.
FNAME_RE = re.compile(r"^(?P<page_id>.+)_seg(?P<seg_idx>\d+)_gt(?P<gt_idx>\d+)\.png$")

all_records = []

for book in TRAIN_BOOKS:
    book_dir = os.path.join(ALIGNED_LINES_DIR, book)
    gt_cache = {}  # page_id -> gt_lines, avoid re-reading the same GT file repeatedly

    for img_path in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(book_dir, "*.png"))):
        filename = os.path.basename(img_path)
        m = FNAME_RE.match(filename)
        if not m:
            print("Skipping unexpected filename:", filename)
            continue

        page_id = m.group("page_id")
        gt_idx = int(m.group("gt_idx"))

        if page_id not in gt_cache:
            gt_path = os.path.join(GT_DIR, book, page_id + ".txt")
            if not os.path.exists(gt_path):
                gt_cache[page_id] = None
                continue
            with open(gt_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
                gt_cache[page_id] = [
                    line.strip() for line in f.read().splitlines() if line.strip()
                ]

        gt_lines = gt_cache[page_id]
        if gt_lines is None or gt_idx >= len(gt_lines):
            continue

        all_records.append({
            "book": book,
            "page": page_id,
            "gt_idx": gt_idx,
            "image_path": img_path,
            "text": gt_lines[gt_idx],

Diagnosed image dimension mismatch between processor and encoder configurations.

Diagnosed image dimension mismatch between processor and encoder configurations.

Done

Root cause

Look back at the load report from the model-assembly cell — it showed the ViTModel.from_pretrained(ENCODER_CKPT) call producing 100% key mismatches (encoder.embeddings.* reported as UNEXPECTED, embeddings.* reported as MISSING). That wasn't a harmless warning — it means the encoder never actually loaded the TrOCR weights. ViTModel.from_pretrained("microsoft/trocr-base-printed") fails silently because that checkpoint is stored as a VisionEncoderDecoderModel with encoder weights nested under an encoder. prefix; asking for a bare ViTModel directly doesn't know to strip that prefix, so it falls back to a randomly-initialized ViT with the default config — which defaults to image_size=224, patch_size=16.

Your image_processor was loaded from the same checkpoint and correctly reports size=384 (TrOCR's real config), so at training time you're feeding 384×384 images into a model that thinks it's a 224×224 ViT. Hence the crash.

This also invalidates the earlier premise of the "TrOCR image encoder gives faster convergence" plan — you've been training with a from-scratch random ViT, not TrOCR's pretrained visual features, this whole time.

Fix

Load the full VisionEncoderDecoderModel checkpoint first (which loads correctly, prefixes intact), then pull the real, correctly-initialized encoder submodule out of it.

Replace the encoder-loading portion of the model-assembly cell:

from transformers import (
    ViTImageProcessor,
    AutoTokenizer,
    AutoModelForCausalLM,
    VisionEncoderDecoderModel,
    VisionEncoderDecoderConfig,
)

ENCODER_CKPT = "microsoft/trocr-base-printed"
DECODER_CKPT = "sagorsarker/bangla-bert-base"

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load the ViT encoder CORRECTLY -- load the full TrOCR
#    VisionEncoderDecoderModel checkpoint (weights are stored
#    with an "encoder." prefix, so ViTModel.from_pretrained()
#    directly on this checkpoint silently fails to map them and
#    falls back to random init at the ViT default config
#    (224x224) -- which is what caused the training crash, since
#    the image_processor for this checkpoint reports size=384).
# ---------------------------------------------------------
image_processor = ViTImageProcessor.from_pretrained(ENCODER_CKPT)

_trocr_full = VisionEncoderDecoderModel.from_pretrained(ENCODER_CKPT)
encoder = _trocr_full.encoder   # real pretrained weights, correct config (384x384)
del _trocr_full                 # drop the TrOCR decoder, we don't need it

print("Encoder image_size after fix:", encoder.config.image_size)
assert encoder.config.image_size == image_processor.size["height"], \
    "Encoder/processor image size mismatch -- do not proceed to training"

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Load Bangla BERT (unchanged)
# ---------------------------------------------------------
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(DECODER_CKPT)
decoder = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(DECODER_CKPT)

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Configure BERT for autoregressive decoding
# ---------------------------------------------------------
decoder.config.is_decoder = True
decoder.config.add_cross_attention = True

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Build VisionEncoderDecoder
# ---------------------------------------------------------
config = VisionEncoderDecoderConfig.from_encoder_decoder_configs(
    encoder.config,
    decoder.config,
)

model = VisionEncoderDecoderModel(
    config=config,
    encoder=encoder,
    decoder=decoder,
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Special tokens
# ---------------------------------------------------------
model.config.decoder_start_token_id = tokenizer.cls_token_id
model.config.pad_token_id = tokenizer.pad_token_id
model.config.eos_token_id = tokenizer.sep_token_id
model.config.vocab_size = model.config.decoder.vocab_size

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Generation configuration

After this fix

Because the encoder now starts from real pretrained TrOCR features instead of random weights, you should expect:

Faster initial convergence than what you'd have seen before (random ViT + random cross-attention was effectively training two randomly-initialized components jointly, which is much harder than one pretrained + one random).

The image_processor and encoder are now guaranteed consistent (asserted at build time), so this specific crash class won't resurface.

Single-GPU OOM fix first

The batch size increase I suggested earlier (16, expecting to match the old 2-GPU throughput) was too aggressive for a single T4's 14.56GB — you're OOMing on the very first step, before gradients even accumulate. A 384×384 ViT encoder + full cross-attention BERT decoder is heavier than it looks, especially with use_cache=False (no KV-cache reuse means more recompute stored for backprop).

Fix: drop batch size, add gradient checkpointing, and raise accumulation to preserve effective batch size.

    output_dir=os.path.join(WORK_DIR, "trocr-bengali-agri"),
    predict_with_generate=True,
    generation_max_length=MAX_TARGET_LEN,

    save_total_limit=2,
    load_best_model_at_end=True,
    metric_for_best_model="cer",
    greater_is_better=False,
    logging_steps=50,
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,       # reduced from 16 -- was OOMing on step 1
    per_device_eval_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=8,       # 4*8 = 32 effective, same as your original target
    gradient_checkpointing=True,         # trade compute for memory -- essential here
    num_train_epochs=15,

Run this cleanup cell, then rebuild trainer with the new training_args before calling trainer.train() again. If batch_size=4 still OOMs, drop to 2 with gradient_accumulation_steps=16 — the effective batch size stays the same either way, only step wall-clock time changes.

Combined with batch_size=4, accumulation=8 (32 micro-steps of overhead per optimizer step) and beam-search generation baked into eval, this compounds badly.

1. Drop gradient checkpointing, raise batch size instead (biggest single win)

2. group_by_length=True needs one more thing to actually work
Seq2SeqTrainer uses group_by_length based on input lengths, but your dataset returns fixed-size pixel_values (images are always the same shape) — the thing that actually varies in length is the labels. For group_by_length to bucket effectively, you need a length column or a way for the trainer to infer per-example length from the dataset. Simplest fix: add a __len__-compatible length attribute to your dataset:

class LineOCRDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, dataframe, image_processor, tokenizer, max_target_len=MAX_TARGET_LEN):
        self.df = dataframe.reset_index(drop=True)
        self.image_processor = image_processor
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.max_target_len = max_target_len
        # precompute text lengths for group_by_length bucketing
        self.lengths = self.df["text"].str.len().tolist()

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.df)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        row = self.df.iloc[idx]
        image = Image.open(row["image_path"]).convert("RGB")
        pixel_values = self.image_processor(image, return_tensors="pt").pixel_values.squeeze(0)
        labels = self.tokenizer(
            row["text"], padding="max_length", max_length=self.max_target_len, truncation=True,
        ).input_ids
        labels = [l if l != self.tokenizer.pad_token_id else -100 for l in labels]
        return {"pixel_values": pixel_values, "labels": torch.tensor(labels)}

train_ds = LineOCRDataset(train_df, image_processor, tokenizer)
val_ds = LineOCRDataset(val_df, image_processor, tokenizer)

Seq2SeqTrainer looks for a .lengths attribute (or length_column_name on a datasets.Dataset) to build the LengthGroupedSampler. With padding="max_length" your labels are already fixed-length in the tensor, so the actual benefit here is smaller than with dynamic padding — if you want the full benefit, switch padding="max_length" to padding=False in __getitem__ and pad dynamically in collate_fn using tokenizer.pad(). That's a bigger change; skip it for now unless step 1 alone isn't enough.

3. Eval is disproportionately expensive — beam search + full eval set every 250 steps
generation_num_beams=4 during periodic eval multiplies the cost of every eval pass roughly 4x versus greedy decoding. Since it/s in your progress bar reflects overall throughput including these periodic eval interruptions, less frequent + cheaper eval helps your wall-clock estimate a lot even though it doesn't touch true training throughput per step. Already reflected above (generation_num_beams=1, eval_steps=500) — you can restore num_beams=4 for a final full evaluation after training completes, on the saved checkpoint, rather than during training.

4. Confirm use_cache=False isn't fighting you unnecessarily during eval generation
model.config.use_cache = False (needed for training) also gets read during generate() at eval time, where caching helps a lot — generation without KV-cache means the model recomputes the entire growing sequence at every decode step instead of reusing past states. Seq2SeqTrainer.evaluate() should temporarily flip this, but it's worth confirming eval isn't silently disabled-cache-during-generation too. If eval steps look disproportionately slow in your logs once training resumes, that's the smoking gun. Nothing to change proactively here — just something to check if step 3 doesn't fully resolve sluggish eval.

Assistant:

8/11/2026 14:58:12

How the numbers were produced

Step 1 — Segment + transcribe. For each page, the segmenter (projection/doctr/tesseract) cut the page image into line-crop candidates. Each crop was then transcribed in isolation by Tesseract (--psm 7, single-line mode) to get a rough hypothesis text for that crop — this transcription is only used as a similarity signal, never as the actual training label.

Step 2 — Build a cost matrix. For a page with N detected crops and M ground-truth lines, an N×M matrix was built where cell (i, j) = CER between crop i's Tesseract transcription and GT line j's true text. Low CER = crop i probably is GT line j.

Step 3 — Sequence alignment (not free matching). Since both crops and GT lines are already in top-to-bottom reading order, this becomes a monotonic alignment problem (Needleman-Wunsch style DP), not "find each crop's best match anywhere." At each step the DP chooses the cheapest of: match crop i↔GT j (cost = CER), skip crop i (fixed penalty), or skip GT j (fixed penalty). This naturally handles a segment that's split into two crops, two segments merged into one crop, or a spurious/missing detection — without needing len(crops) == len(GT) to hold at all.

Step 4 — Count the results.

total_aligned_pairs = every crop↔GT pairing the DP path actually walked through (including bad matches — nothing filtered yet).

accepted_lines = the subset of those pairs whose CER fell under the acceptance threshold you set after inspecting the histograms (the visible valley between the low-CER "real match" cluster and the CER≈1.0 "garbage" spike). Only these become actual training examples — image crop paired with its matched GT text.

So mean/median_cer_all_pairs describes the entire aligned set (signal quality of the alignment itself, garbage included), while accepted_lines is what survives after applying your threshold and becomes usable training data.

Which to go with

Doctr. It has the lowest mean and median CER of the three (0.2375 / 0.1379) and produced the most accepted lines (9,587) despite that stricter quality — meaning its segmentation genuinely aligns better with GT more often, it's not just detecting more low-quality crops. Tesseract is worst on both CER and yield, so drop it as a segmenter (even though it's still your best OCR engine for the transcription-scoring step itself — those are separate roles).

Diagnosed tokenizer vocabulary gaps as benign training artifact.

The vocab-holes warning — not concerning for training

This is a warning from the tokenizer's save_vocabulary() method, not from training itself. It happens because sagorsarker/bangla-bert-base (like most BERT tokenizers) reserves a block of unused vocabulary IDs for future fine-tuning use (e.g. [unused0]...[unused99]-style placeholders), and some of those reserved slots were never filled with actual tokens. When the tokenizer is saved (this happens automatically at each save_steps checkpoint since you passed processing_class=tokenizer to Seq2SeqTrainer), it notices the ID sequence isn't perfectly contiguous and warns.

This is a pre-existing property of that specific checkpoint's vocabulary — not something your training run caused, and not something that will corrupt your model weights or embeddings. The embedding matrix size (vocab_size) already accounts for the full range including the holes, so nothing is being truncated or misaligned.

When it would matter: only if you later modify the vocabulary (add new tokens) and try to save/reload in a way that depends on contiguous indexing. You're not doing that here.

Quick sanity check if you want reassurance:

test_text = "কৃষি বিজ্ঞান পরীক্ষা"
ids = tokenizer(test_text)["input_ids"]
decoded = tokenizer.decode(ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
print(decoded)

If this round-trips correctly, the tokenizer is functioning fine and the warning is cosmetic.

Missing training metrics — this is a Kaggle commit-mode quirk, not a training failure

When you use "Save & Run All" (commit), Kaggle executes the notebook in batch/non-interactive mode, not the live interactive session you were using before. This changes how output renders:

The rich tqdm-based progress bar with the live-updating metrics table (the [ 7/2070 01:32 < ... ] style output you saw interactively) relies on terminal control codes that don't render properly in batch execution — Kaggle's batch runner captures stdout as flat text, so the live-updating widget either doesn't appear or appears as static, hard-to-read fragments.

Your actual Trainer logs (loss, eval metrics) are still being generated at logging_steps=50 — they're just not showing up as the pretty live table. They should still exist as plain print-style log lines in the log output, just formatted differently.

What to do:

Check the actual log output, not just the cell output area — in Kaggle's batch/commit view, look at the "Logs" tab on the notebook version page (separate from the notebook cell rendering). Training logs from Trainer typically get flushed there even when the interactive widget doesn't render.

    logging_steps=50,
    logging_strategy="steps",
    disable_tqdm=True,           # avoid the live widget in batch mode — print plain logs instead
    per_device_train_batch_size=16,
    per_device_eval_batch_size=16,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=2,
    gradient_checkpointing=False,
    num_train_epochs=15,
    learning_rate=5e-5,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    fp16=True,
    dataloader_num_workers=4,
    dataloader_pin_memory=True,
    report_to="none",
)

With disable_tqdm=True, Trainer falls back to plain logger.info()-style output at each logging_steps interval ({'loss': ..., 'learning_rate': ..., 'epoch': ...} as flat printed dicts), which survives batch-mode log capture far more reliably than the live progress bar.

For a persistent, inspectable record independent of Kaggle's log viewer quirks, consider adding report_to="tensorboard" (or keep "none" but manually log to a file):

import logging
logging.basicConfig(
    filename=os.path.join(WORK_DIR, "training.log"),
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s %(message)s",
)

This writes a durable log file inside your Kaggle working directory, which you can view/download after the commit finishes even if the in-browser log viewer is awkward to scroll through for a 10+ hour run.

Bottom line: the run is very likely still training correctly — this is a display/logging-capture artifact of batch execution, not evidence of a stalled or broken job. Check GPU utilization in the commit's resource panel (if Kaggle shows it for background runs) or wait for the first checkpoint save (save_steps=500) and confirm a checkpoint directory actually appears in outputs — that's the most reliable proof the run is progressing.

Diagnosed exposure bias and EOS token misconfiguration, prescribed fixes.

Diagnosed exposure bias and EOS token misconfiguration, prescribed fixes.

Done

Diagnosis: CER/WER > 1 means generation isn't stopping

Training loss near zero + eval loss low, but CER/WER wildly >1 (4.4, meaning ~4x more errors than characters in the reference) is the classic signature of runaway generation — the model isn't emitting EOS during generate(), so it keeps producing tokens up to max_length every single time, turning a short GT line into a long garbage sequence full of insertions.

Look back at your earlier warning log:

"The tokenizer has new PAD/BOS/EOS tokens that differ from the model config and generation config... Updated tokens: {'eos_token_id': None}"

This is the smoking gun. sagorsarker/bangla-bert-base is a BERT tokenizer — it has cls_token/sep_token, not bos_token/eos_token (those attributes are None on the tokenizer itself). When Trainer/transformers auto-reconciles model.generation_config against the tokenizer's special tokens, it saw tokenizer.eos_token_id is None and silently overwrote your manually-set model.config.eos_token_id = tokenizer.sep_token_id back to None in the separate generation_config object that generate() actually reads at eval/inference time.

Result: generate() has no stop condition, decodes to max_length=96 on every validation example, and CER/WER explode from insertion errors — while teacher-forced training loss looks fine because during training the model never has to decide when to stop (labels supply the sequence length).

Fix 1 — force the generation config explicitly, after model creation

Add this right after building model, before creating Seq2SeqTrainingArguments/Trainer (and re-run training from here — the checkpoints you have are likely fine on the training side, just broken for generation):

# CRITICAL FIX: model.generation_config gets silently overwritten to
# eos_token_id=None during Trainer setup, because tokenizer.eos_token_id
# is None (BERT tokenizers use sep_token, not eos_token). Without this,
# generate() never stops and produces max_length garbage on every eval,
# which is why CER/WER were >1 despite near-zero training loss.
model.generation_config.eos_token_id = tokenizer.sep_token_id
model.generation_config.pad_token_id = tokenizer.pad_token_id
model.generation_config.decoder_start_token_id = tokenizer.cls_token_id
model.generation_config.max_length = MAX_TARGET_LEN
model.generation_config.num_beams = 1

# sanity check before training -- these must NOT be None
assert model.generation_config.eos_token_id is not None, "eos_token_id still None!"
print("generation_config:", model.generation_config)

Also re-run this same block right after Seq2SeqTrainer(...) is constructed — Trainer.__init__ re-touches the generation config in some transformers versions, so setting it only before the trainer isn't fully safe:

trainer = Seq2SeqTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=training_args,
    train_dataset=train_ds,
    eval_dataset=val_ds,
    data_collator=collate_fn,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    compute_metrics=compute_metrics,

model.generation_config.pad_token_id = tokenizer.pad_token_id
model.generation_config.decoder_start_token_id = tokenizer.cls_token_id
assert model.generation_config.eos_token_id is not None

Fix 2 — qualitative eval visibility: print actual predictions vs GT each eval

This is the single most useful debugging tool you're missing — numeric CER alone hides what kind of failure you have.

import random
from transformers import TrainerCallback

class QualitativeEvalCallback(TrainerCallback):
    """Prints a handful of actual predictions vs ground truth at every
    evaluation, plus generation-length diagnostics. This is what actually
    tells you whether the model is learning real Bengali OCR or just
    exploiting some degenerate shortcut."""

    def __init__(self, val_dataset, val_df, tokenizer, model, image_processor,
                 n_samples=8, seed=0):
        self.val_dataset = val_dataset
        self.val_df = val_df
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.model = model
        self.image_processor = image_processor
        self.n_samples = n_samples
        self.rng = random.Random(seed)

    def on_evaluate(self, args, state, control, **kwargs):
        model = kwargs.get("model", self.model)
        was_training = model.training
        model.eval()

        idxs = self.rng.sample(range(len(self.val_dataset)), self.n_samples)
        gen_lengths = []

        print(f"\n{'='*100}")
        print(f"QUALITATIVE EVAL SAMPLES -- step {state.global_step}")
        print(f"{'='*100}")

        with torch.no_grad():
            for i in idxs:
                item = self.val_dataset[i]
                pixel_values = item["pixel_values"].unsqueeze(0).to(model.device)

                generated_ids = model.generate(
                    pixel_values=pixel_values,
                    max_length=model.generation_config.max_length,
                    num_beams=1,
                )
                pred_text = self.tokenizer.decode(
                    generated_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True
                )

                gt_text = self.val_df.iloc[i]["text"]
                gen_lengths.append(generated_ids.shape[1])

                cer = char_error_rate(pred_text, gt_text) if "char_error_rate" in globals() else None

                print(f"\n[{i}] GT   : {gt_text}")
                print(f"    PRED : {pred_text}")
                print(f"    gen_len={generated_ids.shape[1]} tokens" +
                      (f"  CER={cer:.3f}" if cer is not None else ""))

        avg_len = sum(gen_lengths) / len(gen_lengths)
        max_len = model.generation_config.max_length
        print(f"\nAvg generated length: {avg_len:.1f} / {max_len} max")
        if avg_len > 0.9 * max_len:
            print("WARNING: generations are near max_length -- EOS is likely "
                  "not being emitted, check generation_config.eos_token_id")
        print(f"{'='*100}\n")

        if was_training:
            model.train()

Add it to the trainer:

qualitative_cb = QualitativeEvalCallback(
    val_dataset=val_ds,
    val_df=val_df,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    model=model,
    image_processor=image_processor,
    n_samples=8,
)

trainer.add_callback(qualitative_cb)

This alone would have caught the EOS bug immediately — you'd have seen 96-token predictions full of repeated garbage next to 10-token GT lines.

Fix 3 — training effectiveness

Beyond the EOS bug, a few things stand out from your metrics:

1. Train loss hit 0.0008 by step 2000 — that's severe overfitting risk, not healthy convergence. With ~7,440 training lines and batch=32, accum=2 (effective 64), 2000 steps is already several epochs over a fairly small, repetitive dataset (agricultural manual text has narrow vocabulary/phrasing). Near-zero training loss this early usually means memorization, not generalization.

from transformers import EarlyStoppingCallback

trainer.add_callback(
    EarlyStoppingCallback(early_stopping_patience=5, early_stopping_threshold=0.001)
)

This stops training once cer stops improving for 5 consecutive evals (2500 steps), rather than blindly running all 15 epochs regardless of whether it's still learning anything useful.

2. Add label smoothing — it's cheap and specifically counters the kind of overconfident-early-collapse you're seeing:

training_args = Seq2SeqTrainingArguments(
    # ... existing args ...
    label_smoothing_factor=0.1,
)

3. Add a warmup ratio — you currently have no warmup, which for a model with a fully randomly-initialized cross-attention block (recall: encoder pretrained, decoder pretrained, but the connection between them is not) can cause unstable early training:

training_args = Seq2SeqTrainingArguments(
    # ... existing args ...
    warmup_ratio=0.05,
    lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
)

4. Lower num_train_epochs — with early stopping in place you don't need to guess, but 15 epochs was likely always too many for this dataset size; consider num_train_epochs=8 as a ceiling so a run that isn't improving doesn't burn 10+ hours needlessly.

8/11/2026 18:49:54

Diagnosed cache compatibility conflict and formulated workaround solution.

Diagnosed cache compatibility conflict and formulated workaround solution.

Done

Root cause: BERT-as-decoder's legacy cache code breaks with transformers' new unified Cache class

This is a different bug from the earlier ones, but related to the same root issue: BertLMHeadModel (used as your decoder) has old-style prepare_inputs_for_generation() code that assumes past_key_values is a legacy tuple-of-tuples and does past_key_values[0][0].shape[2] directly. Current transformers generation code now passes a Cache/DynamicCache/EncoderDecoderCache object instead. When cache gets toggled inconsistently between training (use_cache=False, set earlier for gradient-checkpointing compatibility) and eval-time generate() (which tries to enable caching for decode speed), the decoder receives a malformed/empty cache object partway through decoding, and BERT's old indexing code chokes on it.

This is exactly the kind of interop bug that shows up with "splice a BERT model in as a decoder" architectures — BertLMHeadModel was never designed with the current Cache API in mind, since it predates it.

Fix: disable KV-cache entirely for generation too, not just training

Rather than fighting the interop bug, the clean workaround is to make generation always recompute the full sequence at each decode step (no caching) — slower per-token, but for 96-token max-length lines this is a small, acceptable cost, and it sidesteps the broken code path completely.

Add this right after your generation-config fix block:

# CRITICAL FIX: BertLMHeadModel's prepare_inputs_for_generation() uses
# legacy tuple-based cache indexing (past_key_values[0][0].shape[2]) that
# is incompatible with the newer unified Cache/DynamicCache objects that
# transformers' generate() now produces. This causes an IndexError partway
# through eval-time generation. Rather than patching internals, disable
# KV-cache for generation entirely -- decode is slower (full recompute
# each step) but correct, and acceptable for short 96-token lines.
model.generation_config.eos_token_id = tokenizer.sep_token_id
model.generation_config.pad_token_id = tokenizer.pad_token_id
model.generation_config.decoder_start_token_id = tokenizer.cls_token_id
model.generation_config.use_cache = False   # <-- the actual fix for the IndexError
assert model.generation_config.eos_token_id is not None

And update the qualitative callback's generate() call to match, so it doesn't hit the same crash:

generated_ids = model.generate(
    pixel_values=pixel_values,
    max_length=model.generation_config.max_length,
    num_beams=1,
    use_cache=False,   # match the fix above -- avoids the BertLMHeadModel cache bug
)

import random
from transformers import TrainerCallback, EarlyStoppingCallback

class QualitativeEvalCallback(TrainerCallback):
    def __init__(self, val_dataset, val_df, tokenizer, model, image_processor,
                 n_samples=8, seed=0):
        self.val_dataset = val_dataset
        self.val_df = val_df
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.model = model
        self.image_processor = image_processor
        self.n_samples = n_samples
        self.rng = random.Random(seed)

    def on_evaluate(self, args, state, control, **kwargs):
        model = kwargs.get("model", self.model)
        was_training = model.training
        model.eval()

        idxs = self.rng.sample(range(len(self.val_dataset)), self.n_samples)
        gen_lengths = []

        print(f"\n{'='*100}")
        print(f"QUALITATIVE EVAL SAMPLES -- step {state.global_step}")
        print(f"{'='*100}")

                pixel_values = item["pixel_values"].unsqueeze(0).to(model.device)

                    pixel_values=pixel_values,
                    max_length=model.generation_config.max_length,
                    num_beams=1,
                    use_cache=False,   # avoid BertLMHeadModel legacy-cache IndexError
                )

    EarlyStoppingCallback(early_stopping_patience=5, early_stopping_threshold=0.001)
)

Note on training speed impact

use_cache=False during eval-time generation makes each decode step recompute attention over the full growing sequence instead of reusing cached keys/values — for max_length=96 this means up to ~96x more compute per generated sequence in the worst case (though most lines will hit EOS well before 96 tokens now that the EOS fix from before is also in place, which caps the actual cost). This only affects the periodic eval/generation passes, not training throughput — training forward/backward already runs with use_cache=False regardless, unaffected by this change. Expect eval steps to take noticeably longer than train steps, but this trades off correctness for a modest speed cost, which is the right call here.

8/11/2026 19:17:48

Diagnosed double-shift bug corrupting training signal and generation.

Diagnosed double-shift bug corrupting training signal and generation.

Done

Root cause: a double token-shift corrupts every training example

This explains everything at once: the suspiciously low loss from the very first run (0.0055 at step 500 in your original run, 0.046 here), and the completely empty generations even after fixing EOS and the cache bug.

Here's the mechanism. VisionEncoderDecoderModel.forward(), when you only pass labels (no decoder_input_ids), auto-builds the decoder input by right-shifting the labels:

labels          = [CLS, t1, t2, ..., tn, SEP, PAD, PAD, ...]
decoder_input_ids = shift_right(labels) = [CLS, CLS, t1, t2, ..., tn, SEP, PAD, ...]

It then hands both decoder_input_ids (already shifted) and the original, unshifted labels down to your decoder. The problem: your decoder is BertLMHeadModel, and BertLMHeadModel.forward() also performs its own internal right-shift whenever labels is passed — that's simply how causal-LM loss works in BERT-as-decoder (prediction_scores[:, :-1] vs labels[:, 1:]).

Two shifts compound. The net effect: the model at each position is given context up through token i-1, but asked to predict token i+1 — it never sees the token immediately before the one it's supposed to predict. That's not "hard," it's a corrupted, discontinuous target the model can partially game (hence the too-good-to-be-true loss) but which bears no resemblance to real next-token prediction (hence completely garbage/empty output at inference, since generate() does correct, non-corrupted autoregressive decoding).

This is a known interaction: HuggingFace's own canonical BERT2BERT warm-starting recipe avoids it by passing decoder_input_ids explicitly (the raw, unshifted tokenized target), which bypasses the automatic shift_right entirely and lets BertLMHeadModel's single internal shift be the only shift that happens.

Fix: pass decoder_input_ids explicitly, matching the canonical recipe

from torch.utils.data import Dataset

class LineOCRDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, dataframe, image_processor, tokenizer, max_target_len=MAX_TARGET_LEN):
        self.df = dataframe.reset_index(drop=True)
        self.image_processor = image_processor
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.max_target_len = max_target_len

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.df)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        row = self.df.iloc[idx]
        image = Image.open(row["image_path"]).convert("RGB")
        pixel_values = self.image_processor(image, return_tensors="pt").pixel_values.squeeze(0)

        encoded = self.tokenizer(
            row["text"], padding="max_length", max_length=self.max_target_len, truncation=True,
        )
        input_ids = encoded.input_ids            # [CLS, t1, ..., SEP, PAD, PAD, ...]
        attention_mask = encoded.attention_mask   # 1 for CLS..SEP, 0 for PAD

        # CRITICAL FIX: decoder_input_ids must be the RAW, unshifted tokenized
        # target. BertLMHeadModel performs its own internal right-shift when
        # `labels` is passed (predict token i+1 from context up to token i).
        # If we let VisionEncoderDecoderModel ALSO apply its automatic
        # shift_tokens_right (which happens whenever decoder_input_ids is
        # omitted), the two shifts compound: the model ends up trained to
        # predict token i+1 from context only up to token i-1, skipping the
        # token in between entirely. This corrupted alignment is exactly why
        # training loss looked implausibly low while generation produced
        # empty/garbage output -- the model learned a degenerate shortcut
        # that has nothing to do with real next-token prediction.
        decoder_input_ids = list(input_ids)
        labels = [tok if tok != self.tokenizer.pad_token_id else -100 for tok in input_ids]

        return {
            "pixel_values": pixel_values,
            "decoder_input_ids": torch.tensor(decoder_input_ids),
            "decoder_attention_mask": torch.tensor(attention_mask),
            "labels": torch.tensor(labels),
        }

train_ds = LineOCRDataset(train_df, image_processor, tokenizer)
val_ds = LineOCRDataset(val_df, image_processor, tokenizer)

def collate_fn(batch):
    return {
        "pixel_values": torch.stack([b["pixel_values"] for b in batch]),
        "decoder_input_ids": torch.stack([b["decoder_input_ids"] for b in batch]),
        "decoder_attention_mask": torch.stack([b["decoder_attention_mask"] for b in batch]),
        "labels": torch.stack([b["labels"] for b in batch]),
    }

No changes needed to Seq2SeqTrainer construction — Seq2SeqTrainer.prediction_step() already strips decoder_input_ids/decoder_attention_mask before calling generate() during eval (visible in your earlier traceback: k: v for k, v in inputs.items() if k not in ("decoder_input_ids", "decoder_attention_mask")), so this fix is training-only and doesn't interfere with generation, which was already correctly using decoder_start_token_id from generation_config.

You must rebuild the model from scratch — do not resume from any checkpoint

Every checkpoint saved so far encodes weights fit to the corrupted double-shifted target. Resuming from any of them would just continue training a broken mapping. Re-run the full model-assembly cell (fresh VisionEncoderDecoderModel(...) construction) before restarting trainer.train(). Everything else — the EOS fix, use_cache=False fix, QualitativeEvalCallback, EarlyStoppingCallback — stays as-is; those were correct fixes for genuinely separate bugs, just layered on top of a foundation that was still broken.

What to expect after this fix

Training loss at step 100 should now look much more like a real 102k-vocab classification task in early training — likely in the range of several units, not 0.02–0.05 — and should decrease more gradually over hundreds of steps as cross-attention actually learns to attend to image features. Watch the QualitativeEvalCallback output at the first eval: you should start seeing non-empty, plausibly-Bengali-shaped (if still inaccurate) text rather than blank strings, even if CER is still poor this early. If generations are still empty after this fix, that would point to something else — but this bug is a strong, sufficient explanation for everything observed so far.

from torch.utils.data import Dataset
class LineOCRDataset(Dataset):
    def init(self, dataframe, image_processor, tokenizer, max_target_len=MAX_TARGET_LEN):
        self.df = dataframe.reset_index(drop=True)
        self.image_processor = image_processor
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.max_target_len = max_target_len
    def len(self):
        return len(self.df)
    def getitem(self, idx):
        row = self.df.iloc[idx]
        image = Image.open(row["image_path"]).convert("RGB")
        pixel_values = self.image_processor(image, return_tensors="pt").pixel_values.squeeze(0)
        encoded = self.tokenizer(
            row["text"], padding="max_length", max_length=self.max_target_len, truncation=True,
        )
        input_ids = encoded.input_ids            # [CLS, t1, ..., SEP, PAD, PAD, ...]
        attention_mask = encoded.attention_mask   # 1 for CLS..SEP, 0 for PAD
        # CRITICAL FIX: decoder_input_ids must be the RAW, unshifted tokenized
        # target. BertLMHeadModel performs its own internal right-shift when
        # labels is passed (predict token i+1 from context up to token i).
        # If we let VisionEncoderDecoderModel ALSO apply its automatic
        # shift_tokens_right (which happens whenever decoder_input_ids is
        # omitted), the two shifts compound: the model ends up trained to
        # predict token i+1 from context only up to token i-1, skipping the
        # token in between entirely. This corrupted alignment is exactly why
        # training loss looked implausibly low while generation produced
        # empty/garbage output -- the model learned a degenerate shortcut
        # that has nothing to do with real next-token prediction.
        decoder_input_ids = list(input_ids)
        labels = [tok if tok != self.tokenizer.pad_token_id else -100 for tok in input_ids]
        return {
            "pixel_values": pixel_values,
            "decoder_input_ids": torch.tensor(decoder_input_ids),
            "decoder_attention_mask": torch.tensor(attention_mask),
            "labels": torch.tensor(labels),
        }
train_ds = LineOCRDataset(train_df, image_processor, tokenizer)
val_ds = LineOCRDataset(val_df, image_processor, tokenizer)

import numpy as np
import evaluate
cer_metric = evaluate.load("cer")
wer_metric = evaluate.load("wer")
def compute_metrics(pred):
    labels_ids = pred.label_ids
    pred_ids = pred.predictions
    # defensive: predictions can also carry -100 as a padding marker when generated
    # sequences differ in length across eval batches -- tokenizer.batch_decode doesn't
    # error on this but silently mishandles it, so guard the same way labels are guarded
    pred_ids = np.where(pred_ids != -100, pred_ids, tokenizer.pad_token_id)
    labels_ids = np.where(labels_ids != -100, labels_ids, tokenizer.pad_token_id)
    pred_str = tokenizer.batch_decode(pred_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
    label_str = tokenizer.batch_decode(labels_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
    pairs = [(p, l) for p, l in zip(pred_str, label_str) if l.strip() != ""]
    if not pairs:
        return {"cer": 1.0, "wer": 1.0}
    preds, refs = zip(*pairs)
    cer = cer_metric.compute(predictions=list(preds), references=list(refs))
    wer = wer_metric.compute(predictions=list(preds), references=list(refs))
    return {"cer": cer, "wer": wer}

import random
from transformers import TrainerCallback
class QualitativeEvalCallback(TrainerCallback):
    """Prints a handful of actual predictions vs ground truth at every
    evaluation, plus generation-length diagnostics. This is what actually
    tells you whether the model is learning real Bengali OCR or just
    exploiting some degenerate shortcut."""

def __init__(self, val_dataset, val_df, tokenizer, model, image_processor,
             n_samples=8, seed=0):
    self.val_dataset = val_dataset
    self.val_df = val_df
    self.tokenizer = tokenizer
    self.model = model
    self.image_processor = image_processor
    self.n_samples = n_samples
    self.rng = random.Random(seed)
def on_evaluate(self, args, state, control, **kwargs):
    model = kwargs.get("model", self.model)
    was_training = model.training
    model.eval()
    idxs = self.rng.sample(range(len(self.val_dataset)), self.n_samples)
    gen_lengths = []
    print(f"\n{'='*100}")
    print(f"QUALITATIVE EVAL SAMPLES -- step {state.global_step}")
    print(f"{'='*100}")
    with torch.no_grad():
        for i in idxs:
            item = self.val_dataset[i]
            pixel_values = item["pixel_values"].unsqueeze(0).to(model.device)
            generated_ids = model.generate(
                pixel_values=pixel_values,
                max_length=model.generation_config.max_length,
                num_beams=1,
                use_cache=False,
            )
            pred_text = self.tokenizer.decode(
                generated_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True
            )
            gt_text = self.val_df.iloc[i]["text"]
            gen_lengths.append(generated_ids.shape[1])
            cer = char_error_rate(pred_text, gt_text) if "char_error_rate" in globals() else None
            print(f"\n[{i}] GT   : {gt_text}")
            print(f"    PRED : {pred_text}")
            print(f"    gen_len={generated_ids.shape[1]} tokens" +
                  (f"  CER={cer:.3f}" if cer is not None else ""))
    avg_len = sum(gen_lengths) / len(gen_lengths)
    max_len = model.generation_config.max_length
    print(f"\nAvg generated length: {avg_len:.1f} / {max_len} max")
    if avg_len > 0.9 * max_len:
        print("WARNING: generations are near max_length -- EOS is likely "
              "not being emitted, check generation_config.eos_token_id")
    print(f"{'='*100}\n")
    if was_training:
        model.train()

8/11/2026 19:34:05

Excavated root cause: decoder lacks causal masking and cross-attention.

Excavated root cause: decoder lacks causal masking and cross-attention.

Done

Found it: the decoder was built without causal masking or cross-attention wired in

Look back at a warning buried in your very first model-assembly run:

"[transformers] If you want to use BertLMHeadModel as a standalone, add is_decoder=True."

This warning is definitive proof of the actual bug. AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(DECODER_CKPT) builds BertLMHeadModel's internal BertLayer submodules at load time, using whatever is_decoder/add_cross_attention values are in the checkpoint's config — for sagorsarker/bangla-bert-base (a plain encoder checkpoint), both are False. Each BertLayer's self-attention module caches self.is_decoder = config.is_decoder as a Python instance attribute during construction. Setting decoder.config.is_decoder = True and decoder.config.add_cross_attention = True afterward mutates the config object, but the already-built layers never re-read it — their cached self.is_decoder stays False forever, and no cross-attention submodules were ever created on them in the first place.

The consequence is severe and explains every symptom you've seen across this entire debugging thread:

No cross-attention → the vision encoder's output is completely ignored by the decoder. The model was never conditioned on the image at all.

No causal masking → self-attention is bidirectional. During training, at position i, the model can directly attend to the embedding of the token it's supposed to predict at position i (since we feed the unshifted raw target as decoder_input_ids). It doesn't need to predict anything — it just learns to copy the input through attention + tied embeddings. That's why loss collapses to ~0.004 within 100 steps: it's not learning OCR, it's learning identity.

At real inference time (generate()), there is no future token to leak, no image conditioning ever existed — so the model has learned nothing transferable, and produces empty/garbage output.

This is the actual root cause behind everything, not the earlier shift-doubling bug (which was real and worth fixing, but wasn't the whole story).

Fix: bake is_decoder/add_cross_attention in at load time

from transformers import (
    ViTImageProcessor,
    AutoTokenizer,
    AutoModelForCausalLM,
    VisionEncoderDecoderModel,
    VisionEncoderDecoderConfig,
)

encoder = _trocr_full.encoder
del _trocr_full

assert encoder.config.image_size == image_processor.size["height"]

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(DECODER_CKPT)

# CRITICAL FIX: is_decoder/add_cross_attention MUST be passed at
# from_pretrained() time, not set on .config afterward. BertLayer's
# self-attention caches `self.is_decoder = config.is_decoder` as an
# instance attribute AT CONSTRUCTION TIME, and cross-attention submodules
# are only created if add_cross_attention=True was set when the layers
# were built. Mutating decoder.config after loading does NOT retroactively
# fix already-built layers -- the decoder silently ends up with (a) no
# cross-attention to the image encoder at all, and (b) bidirectional
# (non-causal) self-attention, letting it trivially "cheat" by attending
# directly to the token it's supposed to predict. This is why loss
# collapsed to near-zero almost instantly while real generation produced
# empty/garbage output -- the model never learned OCR, it learned to
# copy its own input.
decoder = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    DECODER_CKPT,
    is_decoder=True,
    add_cross_attention=True,
)

# sanity checks -- do NOT proceed to training if these fail
assert decoder.config.is_decoder is True
first_layer = decoder.bert.encoder.layer[0]
assert first_layer.attention.self.is_decoder is True, \
    "is_decoder not actually applied to layer -- construction order is still wrong"

    "crossattention submodule missing -- add_cross_attention not applied at construction"

    encoder.config,

Every checkpoint so far was built on a decoder with no cross-attention weights and no causal masking — there's no salvaging them. Rebuild the model fresh with the corrected loading, then restart trainer.train().

What to expect this time

With cross-attention weights now genuinely present (randomly initialized, since they're new) and causal masking enforced, initial loss should be much higher than what you've seen so far — likely in the range of several units at step 50–100, reflecting a real 102k-way classification task with no shortcut available — and should decrease gradually over hundreds/thousands of steps as cross-attention actually learns to look at image features. The qualitative eval should start showing non-empty text within the first few hundred steps, even if inaccurate at first; watch for it converging toward recognizable Bengali glyph shapes over time rather than staying blank.

class LineOCRDataset(Dataset):
    def init(self, dataframe, image_processor, tokenizer, max_target_len=MAX_TARGET_LEN):
        self.df = dataframe.reset_index(drop=True)
        self.image_processor = image_processor
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.max_target_len = max_target_len
    def len(self):
        return len(self.df)
    def getitem(self, idx):
        row = self.df.iloc[idx]
        image = Image.open(row["image_path"]).convert("RGB")
        pixel_values = self.image_processor(image, return_tensors="pt").pixel_values.squeeze(0)
        encoded = self.tokenizer(
            row["text"], padding="max_length", max_length=self.max_target_len, truncation=True,
        )
        input_ids = encoded.input_ids            # [CLS, t1, ..., SEP, PAD, PAD, ...]
        attention_mask = encoded.attention_mask   # 1 for CLS..SEP, 0 for PAD
        # CRITICAL FIX: decoder_input_ids must be the RAW, unshifted tokenized
        # target. BertLMHeadModel performs its own internal right-shift when
        # labels is passed (predict token i+1 from context up to token i).
        # If we let VisionEncoderDecoderModel ALSO apply its automatic
        # shift_tokens_right (which happens whenever decoder_input_ids is
        # omitted), the two shifts compound: the model ends up trained to
        # predict token i+1 from context only up to token i-1, skipping the
        # token in between entirely. This corrupted alignment is exactly why
        # training loss looked implausibly low while generation produced
        # empty/garbage output -- the model learned a degenerate shortcut
        # that has nothing to do with real next-token prediction.
        decoder_input_ids = list(input_ids)
        labels = [tok if tok != self.tokenizer.pad_token_id else -100 for tok in input_ids]
        return {
            "pixel_values": pixel_values,
            "decoder_input_ids": torch.tensor(decoder_input_ids),
            "decoder_attention_mask": torch.tensor(attention_mask),
            "labels": torch.tensor(labels),
        }

import numpy as np
import evaluate
cer_metric = evaluate.load("cer")
wer_metric = evaluate.load("wer")
def compute_metrics(pred):
    labels_ids = pred.label_ids
    pred_ids = pred.predictions
    # defensive: predictions can also carry -100 as a padding marker when generated
    # sequences differ in length across eval batches -- tokenizer.batch_decode doesn't
    # error on this but silently mishandles it, so guard the same way labels are guarded
    pred_ids = np.where(pred_ids != -100, pred_ids, tokenizer.pad_token_id)
    labels_ids = np.where(labels_ids != -100, labels_ids, tokenizer.pad_token_id)
    pred_str = tokenizer.batch_decode(pred_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
    label_str = tokenizer.batch_decode(labels_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
    pairs = [(p, l) for p, l in zip(pred_str, label_str) if l.strip() != ""]
    if not pairs:
        return {"cer": 1.0, "wer": 1.0}
    preds, refs = zip(*pairs)
    cer = cer_metric.compute(predictions=list(preds), references=list(refs))
    wer = wer_metric.compute(predictions=list(preds), references=list(refs))
    return {"cer": cer, "wer": wer}

def on_evaluate(self, args, state, control, **kwargs):

    model.eval()

            gen_lengths.append(generated_ids.shape[1])
            cer = char_error_rate(pred_text, gt_text) if "char_error_rate" in globals() else None
            print(f"\n[{i}] GT   : {gt_text}")
            print(f"    PRED : {pred_text}")
            print(f"    gen_len={generated_ids.shape[1]} tokens" +
                  (f"  CER={cer:.3f}" if cer is not None else ""))
    avg_len = sum(gen_lengths) / len(gen_lengths)

The training loss going to zero while generation produces empty output is the giveaway: the model is exploiting teacher forcing rather than learning to generate.

Root cause: decoder_input_ids is being fed the raw, unshifted target sequence, so the model is trained to see its own answer at every position.

VisionEncoderDecoderModel.forward uses decoder_input_ids exactly as given — no internal shift happens there. The shifting only happens automatically when decoder_input_ids is omitted and labels is passed. In this dataset code, decoder_input_ids = list(input_ids) (the same sequence as labels, just without the -100 masking). So at every timestep t, the decoder is handed input_ids[t] as input and asked to predict labels[t] = input_ids[t] — with causal masking, it can still see position t itself as input (BERT-style embeddings aren't shifted by attention masking alone; the token at position t is literally in the input at position t). It trivially learns identity copy → loss collapses near zero → at real inference time (generate, no teacher forcing) it has never learned actual next-token prediction from image features, so it emits garbage/empty output almost immediately (EOS or degenerate short output).

The comment block in the code claims the opposite (that double-shifting is the bug) — that reasoning is backwards. BertLMHeadModel does not silently re-shift when explicit decoder_input_ids are passed to a VisionEncoderDecoderModel — shifting is the encoder-decoder wrapper's job, done only when you don't supply decoder_input_ids yourself. Here you are supplying them, unshifted, so no shift happens anywhere. That's the actual defect.

Fix — build decoder_input_ids as the right-shifted sequence (start token + input_ids[:-1]), not a copy of input_ids:

from transformers.models.bert.modeling_bert import BertLMHeadModel  # noqa (context only)

def __getitem__(self, idx):
    row = self.df.iloc[idx]
    image = Image.open(row["image_path"]).convert("RGB")
    pixel_values = self.image_processor(image, return_tensors="pt").pixel_values.squeeze(0)

    encoded = self.tokenizer(
        row["text"], padding="max_length", max_length=self.max_target_len, truncation=True,
    )
    input_ids = encoded.input_ids            # [CLS, t1, ..., SEP, PAD, PAD, ...]

    # labels: what the model must predict at each position, PAD masked to -100
    labels = [tok if tok != self.tokenizer.pad_token_id else -100 for tok in input_ids]

    # decoder_input_ids: RIGHT-SHIFTED version of input_ids.
    # Position t must NOT be able to see labels[t] as its own input.
    decoder_start_token_id = self.tokenizer.cls_token_id
    decoder_input_ids = [decoder_start_token_id] + input_ids[:-1]

    # attention mask must correspond to the shifted decoder_input_ids, not the raw encoding
    decoder_attention_mask = [1 if tok != self.tokenizer.pad_token_id else 0
                               for tok in decoder_input_ids]

    return {
        "pixel_values": pixel_values,
        "decoder_input_ids": torch.tensor(decoder_input_ids),
        "decoder_attention_mask": torch.tensor(decoder_attention_mask),
        "labels": torch.tensor(labels),
    }

Equivalently, and more robustly (uses HF's own tested shift logic instead of a hand-rolled one), drop decoder_input_ids/decoder_attention_mask from the dataset entirely and let the model shift internally:

# In the Dataset: only return pixel_values and labels
return {
    "pixel_values": pixel_values,
    "labels": torch.tensor(labels),
}

# In collate_fn: don't stack decoder_input_ids/decoder_attention_mask
def collate_fn(batch):
    return {
        "pixel_values": torch.stack([b["pixel_values"] for b in batch]),
        "labels": torch.stack([b["labels"] for b in batch]),
    }

With no explicit decoder_input_ids, VisionEncoderDecoderModel.forward calls shift_tokens_right(labels, pad_token_id, decoder_start_token_id) itself, guaranteeing correct alignment — this is the recommended usage pattern and removes the whole class of bug.

Either fix, combined with model.config.decoder_start_token_id = tokenizer.cls_token_id (already set), should make loss decrease more slowly/realistically and generation start producing real text within a few hundred steps.

Diagnosed performance bottlenecks beyond precision; recommended validation tests.

Diagnosed performance bottlenecks beyond precision; recommended validation tests.

Done

fp16 isn't why it's slow — it should be making things faster, not slower. Mixed precision on a Tensor Core GPU normally cuts step time significantly versus fp32. If your GPU is Ampere/Hopper (A100, RTX 30/40-series, H100), you could try bf16=True instead of fp16=True — it skips the loss-scaling machinery fp16 needs and is a bit more numerically stable for transformer training — but that's a minor win, not a fix for "training takes too much time."

The real time sinks in this config are two things unrelated to precision:

1. model.gradient_checkpointing_enable() is called unconditionally on the model, overriding gradient_checkpointing=False in training_args. Checkpointing trades ~20-30% more compute (it recomputes activations on the backward pass) for lower memory. Since you called it directly on the model object, it's active regardless of what TrainingArguments says. If you're not memory-constrained, drop the manual call and let training_args control it:

# Remove this line if VRAM allows — it's silently overriding gradient_checkpointing=False
# model.gradient_checkpointing_enable()

2. use_cache=False is forced everywhere, including generation during eval. With predict_with_generate=True and eval_steps=100, the trainer runs full autoregressive generation (up to 96 tokens/sample) over your entire eval set every 100 steps — and without KV caching, each generated token re-runs attention over the whole growing sequence from scratch, making generation roughly O(n²) instead of O(n). The QualitativeEvalCallback adds 8 more uncached generate() calls on top of that, every eval step. This is very likely your dominant cost, not fp16.

Worth checking: was use_cache=False actually required because of a caching bug in this hacked-together BERT-as-causal-decoder, or was it a workaround for symptoms of the decoder_input_ids leakage bug (e.g., an IndexError that happened because the model was generating pathologically, like immediate EOS/degenerate output)? Now that the shift is fixed, it's worth re-testing with use_cache=True — if it no longer errors, you likely get a large speedup on eval generation for free. If it still throws the IndexError, then it's a real bug in how add_cross_attention interacts with BERT's cache implementation and you're stuck with False for generation.

Cheaper mitigations either way: raise eval_steps (e.g. 200-500) so full generation runs less often, or shrink the eval set specifically for predict_with_generate (keep a small fixed subset for CER/WER tracking, run loss-only eval more frequently on the rest).

Yes — you should never let a full run tell you whether the wiring is correct. Two checks catch this class of bug in minutes, before spending any real compute:

A. Assert the shift is actually right, directly on a batch:

batch = train_ds[0]
decoder_input_ids = batch["decoder_input_ids"].tolist()
labels = batch["labels"].tolist()

assert decoder_input_ids[0] == tokenizer.cls_token_id
for t in range(1, len(labels)):
    if labels[t - 1] != -100:  # skip pad positions
        assert decoder_input_ids[t] == labels[t - 1], (
            f"Misaligned at t={t}: decoder_input_ids[t]={decoder_input_ids[t]} "
            f"should equal labels[t-1]={labels[t-1]}"
        )
print("Shift alignment OK")

If this passes, position t's input can no longer equal position t's target — the identity-copy shortcut is structurally impossible.

B. Overfit a tiny slice and generate for real (no teacher forcing) — this is the standard seq2seq pipeline sanity check, and it would have caught this bug in ~2 minutes instead of a full training run:

tiny_ds = torch.utils.data.Subset(train_ds, range(8))
tiny_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(tiny_ds, batch_size=8, collate_fn=collate_fn)
batch = next(iter(tiny_loader))
batch = {k: v.to(model.device) for k, v in batch.items()}

optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=5e-5)
model.train()
for step in range(300):
    out = model(**batch)
    out.loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    if step % 50 == 0:
        print(step, out.loss.item())

# Now the real test: no teacher forcing at all
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    gen = model.generate(pixel_values=batch["pixel_values"], max_length=MAX_TARGET_LEN,
                          num_beams=1, use_cache=False)
for i in range(4):
    print("PRED:", tokenizer.decode(gen[i], skip_special_tokens=True))
    print("GT  :", tokenizer.decode(batch["labels"][i][batch["labels"][i] != -100], skip_special_tokens=True))

If the model can drive loss down and generate() reproduces those 8 lines reasonably well, the shift, cross-attention wiring, and generation config are all sound — you can trust the full run. If loss collapses instantly (within the first ~10-20 steps, way before 8 examples could plausibly be memorized) while generate() still outputs garbage/empty, that's the leakage signature again, and you go looking at the data pipeline, not hyperparameters.

A cheap third check worth adding to (B): feed a zeroed/blank pixel_values tensor into the same overfit-trained model and confirm the predictions get noticeably worse. If they don't change, the decoder is ignoring the encoder entirely (cross-attention not actually contributing), which is a separate failure mode from the shift bug and wouldn't show up in the shift assertion.

What the logs actually show:

Signs the fix from before is working correctly:

Loss is descending smoothly (7.5 → 3.8 over 200 steps) instead of collapsing near-zero in the first few steps — that's the signature of real learning, not the identity-copy shortcut.

avg_len is falling steadily: 96 → 61.6 → 18.6 → 19.0. That means the model is learning to emit EOS instead of running to max_length every time — direct evidence the decoder-shift fix took effect (before, EOS was never learned because the model was cheating).

CER even dipped to ~0.78 at step 150 before drifting back up slightly — noisy but broadly consistent with a model that's starting to extract signal from the image.

The genuinely suspicious pattern:
At steps 150–200, several different ground-truth lines from different images produce nearly the same output phrase — e.g. "এই সকল সথানের জনয ভমি বযবহার করা হয" shows up for GT indices 633, 545, and 616, which have completely unrelated ground truth. That's not random noise; it's the model outputting a fixed high-frequency phrase regardless of the input image.

There are two explanations, and they point to very different next steps:

Benign / expected at this stage: your decoder is initialized from bangla-bert-base, a full pretrained Bengali language model. Its self-attention/LM weights already encode strong Bengali "what word tends to follow what" priors. Cross-attention to the vision encoder, on the other hand, is randomly initialized — it starts at zero informational value and has to be learned from scratch. It's completely normal, in TrOCR-style training, for the model to spend its first several hundred steps producing plausible-looking Bengali that's only weakly conditioned on the image (falling back to whatever's most frequent/likely under the decoder's own LM prior) before cross-attention "wins" and starts actually reading the image. You're at step 200 of 1104 (only ~1.6 of 8 epochs) — this window is exactly where you'd expect that transitional garbage.

A real bug: image/text misalignment. If train_df/val_df were built by joining an image-path list and a text list that weren't sorted/matched identically (e.g., os.listdir() order not guaranteed to match a separately-loaded transcript list, or a merge/sort applied to one but not the other), the model would be looking at image A while being trained to predict the transcript of image B. This produces exactly this symptom: outputs that never track the actual image content, and it will not resolve with more training steps, no matter how long you wait.

The fastest way to tell these apart is a direct visual check, which is what you're asking for — but I'd also do the even-cheaper version outside training first, since it doesn't require waiting for a checkpoint:

# Run this once, standalone, before trusting anything else
import random

    ax.axis("off")
    print(f"[{i}] {row['image_path']}\n     text: {row['text']}\n")

Look at each image and read the Bengali line yourself — does it match row["text"]? If even one is visibly wrong, stop training and fix the dataframe construction (check whatever code built image_path/text columns — sorting, glob() order, a join key mismatch, etc.) before spending more compute.

Callback with image loading, including both the raw image and the actual normalized tensor the model receives — showing both matters because a raw-image check only catches a dataframe-alignment bug, while showing the denormalized pixel_values also catches a preprocessing bug (wrong crop, channel swap, or corrupted resize) that wouldn't show up any other way:

import random
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from PIL import Image
from transformers import TrainerCallback

class QualitativeEvalCallback(TrainerCallback):
    """Prints predictions vs ground truth at every evaluation, and now also
    renders the raw image plus the denormalized tensor actually fed to the
    model -- lets you visually confirm image/text alignment and catch
    preprocessing bugs, not just decoding bugs."""

    def __init__(self, val_dataset, val_df, tokenizer, model, image_processor,
                 n_samples=8, seed=0, show_images=True):
        self.val_dataset = val_dataset
        self.val_df = val_df
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.model = model
        self.image_processor = image_processor
        self.n_samples = n_samples
        self.rng = random.Random(seed)
        self.show_images = show_images

    def _denormalize(self, pixel_values):
        # Reverse ViTImageProcessor's normalization to see what the model
        # actually receives (as opposed to the raw file on disk).
        mean = torch.tensor(self.image_processor.image_mean).view(3, 1, 1)
        std = torch.tensor(self.image_processor.image_std).view(3, 1, 1)
        img = pixel_values.detach().cpu() * std + mean
        return img.clamp(0, 1).permute(1, 2, 0).numpy()

    def on_evaluate(self, args, state, control, **kwargs):
        model = kwargs.get("model", self.model)
        was_training = model.training
        model.eval()
        idxs = self.rng.sample(range(len(self.val_dataset)), self.n_samples)
        gen_lengths = []
        print(f"\n{'='*100}")
        print(f"QUALITATIVE EVAL SAMPLES -- step {state.global_step}")
        print(f"{'='*100}")

        if self.show_images:
            n = len(idxs)
            fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, n, figsize=(3 * n, 6))
            if n == 1:
                axes = axes.reshape(2, 1)

        with torch.no_grad():
            for col, i in enumerate(idxs):
                item = self.val_dataset[i]
                pixel_values = item["pixel_values"].unsqueeze(0).to(model.device)
                generated_ids = model.generate(
                    pixel_values=pixel_values,
                    max_length=model.generation_config.max_length,
                    num_beams=1,
                    use_cache=False,
                )
                pred_text = self.tokenizer.decode(
                    generated_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True
                )
                row = self.val_df.iloc[i]
                gt_text = row["text"]
                gen_lengths.append(generated_ids.shape[1])

                print(f"\n[{i}] IMG  : {row['image_path']}")
                print(f"    GT   : {gt_text}")
                print(f"    PRED : {pred_text}")
                print(f"    gen_len={generated_ids.shape[1]} tokens")

                if self.show_images:
                    # Row 1: raw file from disk -- catches dataframe/path misalignment
                    raw_img = Image.open(row["image_path"]).convert("RGB")
                    axes[0, col].imshow(raw_img)
                    axes[0, col].set_title(f"idx {i} (raw)", fontsize=8)
                    axes[0, col].axis("off")

                    # Row 2: what the model actually saw -- catches preprocessing bugs
                    proc_img = self._denormalize(item["pixel_values"])
                    axes[1, col].imshow(proc_img)
                    axes[1, col].set_title("model input", fontsize=8)
                    axes[1, col].axis("off")

        if self.show_images:
            plt.tight_layout()
            plt.show()

        avg_len = sum(gen_lengths) / len(gen_lengths)
        max_len = model.generation_config.max_length
        print(f"\nAvg generated length: {avg_len:.1f} / {max_len} max")
        if avg_len > 0.9 * max_len:
            print("WARNING: generations are near max_length -- EOS is likely "
                  "not being emitted, check generation_config.eos_token_id")
        print(f"{'='*100}\n")
        if was_training:
            model.train()

Two things to look at once this runs: whether the "raw" row's visible Bengali text matches the printed GT (misalignment check), and whether the "model input" row looks like a sane, undistorted version of the same image (preprocessing check) — if the raw image is fine but the model-input row looks cropped wrong, flipped, or blank, that's a bug in image_processor usage rather than the dataframe.

If both rows check out across several samples and the repeated-phrase pattern is still present by ~step 500–800, that's the point to treat it as a real training problem (e.g., cross-attention not learning, encoder features not informative) rather than an early-training artifact — worth revisiting then rather than now.

Analyzed model's line-level architecture limitations and inference requirements.

Done

Yes — you need to segment the held-out book into lines the same way, using the same pipeline.

This model is a line-level OCR model (like TrOCR): it expects one text line per image, resized/normalized to a single 384×384-ish crop via ViTImageProcessor. It has no notion of multi-line layout, reading order, or line detection — cross-attention was only ever trained to map "one line's worth of glyphs" → "one line's transcript."

If you feed it a full page:

The image gets squashed/cropped to whatever the encoder expects, destroying most of the multi-line content.

Even if it didn't, the model has never seen more than one line's worth of text per image at training time — output would be out-of-distribution garbage, not a real page transcription.

So: run the same line-segmentation step on the held-out book, produce (image_path, gt_text) pairs exactly as you did for train/val, and evaluate on that. If you eventually want true full-page inference, that's a separate problem (a line-detection/segmentation model feeding crops into this OCR model, i.e. a two-stage pipeline) — this model alone isn't the right tool for whole-page input.

Evaluated alternative architectures and alignment strategies over line-level segmentation.

Done

Given your constraints, yes — the manual line segmentation was the expensive step, and it wasn't strictly necessary. A few things worth having tried instead:

1. Segmentation-free fine-tuning (Donut). Donut takes a whole page image and generates the transcript directly — no line boxes needed at all, just (page_image, page_text) pairs, which is exactly the data you already had. This sidesteps the entire segmentation problem rather than working around it. Main caveat: very dense pages may exceed a reasonable decoder context length, so you might need paragraph-level chunks rather than true full-page for the densest scans — but that's a much cheaper split than manual line segmentation.

2. Auto-align instead of hand-segment. Run Tesseract's own layout engine to detect line boxes on the pages (it already segments reasonably, even where its recognition is mediocre), then use edit-distance/DP sequence alignment between Tesseract's noisy line-level output and your page-level GT to automatically assign each detected line the correct GT substring. This is standard practice for OCR ground-truthing (same idea used by OCR-D/Ocropus pipelines) and would likely have recovered most of the ~4,500 lines you dropped, without manual verification — usable either for TrOCR fine-tuning or, more usefully, as training pairs for step 3.

3. Double down on LLM correction instead of training an OCR model. Your numbers already show this is your best lever (WER 0.384 → 0.289 with Qwen-14B, essentially free). The same alignment trick in (2) gives you a large (tesseract_raw, gt) corpus with zero segmentation effort. Use that to fine-tune (LoRA) a corrector on your domain vocabulary (soil-science/agriculture terms, common conjunct-script error patterns) instead of relying on a generic zero-shot 14B prompt — that's very likely to beat both your line-level TrOCR model and your current correction numbers, for a fraction of the time you spent segmenting lines.

If you're time-constrained, I'd prioritize (3) now, since Tesseract+correction is already your leader, and treat (1)/(2) as what to reach for next time you have page-level-only GT.

Yes, this is very feasible — page-level GT with no line boxes is exactly the input Donut expects. Since you already have (page_image, page_text) pairs directly from your pages/ and ground-truth-ocr/ folders, there's no segmentation step needed at all.

Two caveats worth knowing before you run this: (1) Donut's decoder tokenizer is a generic multilingual SentencePiece vocab (not Bengali-specialized like bangla-bert-base), so Bengali may tokenize into more, smaller pieces — watch it in the qualitative samples; (2) full pages are much bigger tensors than line crops, so batch size has to drop and gradient accumulation compensates — adjust IMAGE_SIZE/per_device_train_batch_size down further if you hit OOM.

# Cell 1
