Loader code:

"""Stage 1 — load scanned page-images"""
from __future__ import annotations
from ..contracts import *  # noqa
from ..data import validate
from ..data import snapshot
from pathlib import Path
from pdf2image import convert_from_path

IMAGE_EXTS = {".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".tif", ".tiff"}

def _cfg_get(cfg: dict, key: str, default):
    return cfg.get("ingest", {}).get(key, default)

def _render_pdfs_to_pages(raw_root: Path, pages_root: Path, dpi: int) -> None:
    pages_root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for pdf_path in sorted(raw_root.glob("*.pdf")):
        doc_id = pdf_path.stem
        out_dir = pages_root / doc_id
        out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

        if any(out_dir.glob("*.png")):
            continue

        images = convert_from_path(str(pdf_path), dpi=dpi)
        for i, img in enumerate(images, start=1):
            out_path = out_dir / f"page-{i:03d}.png"
            if not out_path.exists():
                img.save(out_path, "PNG")

def _iter_pages(pages_root: Path) -> list[Page]:
    pages: list[Page] = []
    if not pages_root.exists():
        return pages
    for doc_dir in sorted(p for p in pages_root.iterdir() if p.is_dir()):
        for image_path in sorted(p for p in doc_dir.rglob("*") if p.suffix.lower() in IMAGE_EXTS):
            page_id = f"{doc_dir.name}:{image_path.stem}"
            pages.append(Page(id=page_id, image_path=str(image_path), doc_id=doc_dir.name))
    return pages

def load_pages(cfg: dict) -> list[Page]:
    """Read PDFs from data/raw, render to data/pages, then return page-image records."""
    data_root = Path(_cfg_get(cfg, "data_root", "data"))
    raw_root = data_root / _cfg_get(cfg, "raw_dir", "raw")
    pages_root = data_root / _cfg_get(cfg, "pages_dir", "pages")
    dpi = int(_cfg_get(cfg, "render_dpi", 150))

    _render_pdfs_to_pages(raw_root, pages_root, dpi)
    pages = _iter_pages(pages_root)
    if not pages:
        raise ValueError(f"No page images found under {pages_root}. Ensure PDFs exist in {raw_root}.")
    
    validate(pages)
    snapshot(data_root) 
    
    return pages

Then the preprocessor runs - it mainly detects the blank pages for now.

Preprocessor code:

"""Stage 1 — deskew / denoise / binarize / augment"""
from __future__ import annotations
from ..contracts import *  # noqa
from pathlib import Path

import cv2
import numpy as np

IMAGE_EXTS = {".png", ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".tif", ".tiff"}

def _cfg_get(cfg: dict, key: str, default):
    return cfg.get("ingest", {}).get(key, default)

def _page_stats(image_path: Path, min_blob_area: int) -> dict:
    img = cv2.imread(str(image_path), cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
    if img is None:
        raise ValueError(f"OpenCV could not read {image_path}")
    _, binary = cv2.threshold(img, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY_INV + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)
    kernel = np.ones((2, 2), np.uint8)
    cleaned = cv2.morphologyEx(binary, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, kernel)
    _num_labels, _labels, stats, _centroids = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(cleaned, connectivity=8)
    areas = stats[1:, cv2.CC_STAT_AREA]
    real_blobs = areas[areas >= min_blob_area]
    total_pixels = img.shape[0] * img.shape[1]
    ink_ratio = float(real_blobs.sum()) / total_pixels if total_pixels else 0.0
    return {"blob_count": int(len(real_blobs)), "ink_ratio": ink_ratio}

def _is_blank(stats: dict, min_blob_count: int, ink_ratio_threshold: float) -> bool:
    return stats["blob_count"] < min_blob_count or stats["ink_ratio"] < ink_ratio_threshold

def run(pages: list[Page], cfg: dict) -> list[Page]:
    """Filter likely-blank page-images; splitting/rendering is handled by loader.load_pages()."""
    data_root = Path(_cfg_get(cfg, "data_root", "data"))
    blank_root = data_root / _cfg_get(cfg, "blank_dir", "blank")

    min_blob_area = int(_cfg_get(cfg, "min_blob_area", 15))
    ink_ratio_threshold = float(_cfg_get(cfg, "ink_ratio_threshold", 0.002))
    min_blob_count = int(_cfg_get(cfg, "min_blob_count", 3))

    blank_root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    processed: list[Page] = []
    for page in pages:
        doc_id = page.doc_id
        image_path = Path(page.image_path)
        stats = _page_stats(image_path, min_blob_area=min_blob_area)
        if _is_blank(stats, min_blob_count=min_blob_count, ink_ratio_threshold=ink_ratio_threshold):
            dest_dir = blank_root / doc_id
            dest_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            dest_path = dest_dir / image_path.name
            image_path.replace(dest_path)
            continue

        processed.append(page)

    return processed

Your two questions

Optimizer file — yes, skip it. For inference you only need: config.json, generation_config.json, model.safetensors, tokenizer_config.json, spiece.model, special_tokens_map.json. Drop optimizer.pt, scheduler.pt, rng_state.pth, trainer_state.json — that alone takes you from ~6.7GB to ~2.3GB.

Doesn't affect inference speed (the final vocab projection costs the same either way), just wastes ~1GB on disk. Optional cleanup, not required:

model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained("checkpoint-2200")
model.config.tie_word_embeddings = True
model.tie_weights()
model.save_pretrained("checkpoint-2200-tied", safe_serialization=True)

CPU speed — honestly, don't guess, but I've designed ocr.py around the answer either way. A ~300M-param encoder-decoder doing sequential one-line-at-a-time generate() calls on CPU would genuinely be a bottleneck at your corpus scale. The single biggest lever is batching multiple lines into one generate() call instead of one-by-one — this is not a minor tweak, it's the difference between "fine" and "too slow," so I built the ocr.py below to always batch corpus-wide rather than per-region. You still have an unreported number from the CPU-latency cell I gave you earlier — run that before shipping, since it tells you the real per-line cost on your actual target machine. If it's still too slow after batching, next lever is dynamic int8 quantization (torch.quantization.quantize_dynamic on the Linear layers, or an ONNX export via optimum), typically 2-4x on CPU for models this size.

loader.py / preprocess.py — quick read

Both are fine; two things worth knowing rather than fixing:

Page.id is built as "<doc_id>:<page_stem>" (colon-joined) — this matters for ocr.py below, since I need to split it back apart to find the matching page image and GT file.

preprocess.run() physically moves blank pages out of pages/ into blank/ — meaning on any re-run, blank pages are already gone from the source dir. Not a bug, just means "the full corpus" shrinks permanently after the first run.

Enhancement — recommend leaving it off

Every transform in your sweep is either a no-op (grayscale/contrast_stretch/deskew match raw exactly — Tesseract already normalizes these internally) or actively harmful, often badly (morph_erode: CER 0.47 vs raw's 0.13 — Bengali's thin conjunct strokes and multi-level diacritics don't survive binarization/morphology). upscale_2x is the closest to a real win (better CER on 2/3 books), but the margins (1–3% relative) are smaller than the noise your own corpus already demonstrated: CER moved from 0.1322 to 0.1611 (+22% relative) just going from the 15-page sample to the full corpus. A sweep this size on a sample that small isn't reliable enough to trust as a default.

"""Stage 1 — ENHANCEMENT (VAE / diffusion) — generative denoise / super-resolution of degraded scans"""
from __future__ import annotations
from ..contracts import *  # noqa

# Sweep found nothing worth shipping -- see notes in chat. Left OFF by
# default (set cfg["enhance"]["enabled"] = False). The upscale_2x hook
# below is wired but inactive; only flip it on for a specific book after
# re-validating on the FULL corpus, not the 15-page sample that produced
# these numbers.

import cv2
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image

def _to_cv(pil_img: Image.Image) -> np.ndarray:
    return cv2.cvtColor(np.array(pil_img.convert("RGB")), cv2.COLOR_RGB2BGR)

def _to_pil(cv_img: np.ndarray) -> Image.Image:
    if cv_img.ndim == 2:
        return Image.fromarray(cv_img)
    return Image.fromarray(cv2.cvtColor(cv_img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB))

def _upscale_2x(pil_img: Image.Image) -> Image.Image:
    cv_img = _to_cv(pil_img)
    h, w = cv_img.shape[:2]
    return _to_pil(cv2.resize(cv_img, (w * 2, h * 2), interpolation=cv2.INTER_CUBIC))

class Enhancer:
    """No learned (VAE/diffusion) enhancer implemented -- the classical
    sweep found no transform worth deploying, learned or otherwise."""

    def __init__(self, cfg: dict) -> None:
        self.cfg = cfg["enhance"]
        self._apply_upscale_for: set[str] = set()  # e.g. {"Krishi-Bigyan"} once validated

    def train(self, pages: list[Page]) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError("No learned enhancer implemented")

    def apply(self, pages: list[Page]) -> list[Page]:
        if not self._apply_upscale_for:
            return pages
        for page in pages:
            if page.doc_id in self._apply_upscale_for:
                img = Image.open(page.image_path).convert("RGB")
                _upscale_2x(img).save(page.image_path)
        return pages

def run(pages: list[Page], cfg: dict) -> list[Page]:
    if not cfg["enhance"]["enabled"]:
        return pages
    return Enhancer(cfg).apply(pages)

Set cfg["enhance"]["enabled"] = False in your config.

Layout → OCR: one structural gap worth knowing about

Your mT5 corrector was trained on single-line crops (mean 30 / max 44 tokens). layout.py's YOLO regions are whole paragraph/table/heading blocks — much longer, out of distribution for the corrector, and would silently truncate against MAX_LENGTH=96. I handle this in ocr.py by running Tesseract at the region level (psm 6 for multi-line blocks), then splitting Tesseract's own line breaks back into individual lines before correction — this keeps mT5's input shape matching training, regardless of how coarse the upstream region is. It's not a perfect match to your original doctr-cropped training lines (different crop boundaries), but it's much closer than feeding whole paragraphs in. Table regions get the same line-split-and-correct treatment as text, as an approximation — I don't have a real cell-flattening step for raw Tesseract table crops (that needs table-structure recognition, out of scope here); flagging this rather than pretending it's solved.

Also: Region (per every call site I can see) only carries page_id/bbox/kind — no image path. I reconstruct the path from page_id + your pages_dir convention. This works today but is fragile if enhance.py ever starts writing to a different location — if you want to harden it later, having layout.detect() attach image_path to each Region directly would remove the guesswork.

One more inference I had to make without seeing contracts.py: I constructed Chunk(page_id=..., bbox=..., kind=..., text=...), mirroring Region's shape. Check this matches your actual Chunk fields — adjust names if not.

"""Stage 3 — OCR/HTR (BASELINE = pretrained foundation, fine-tuned)"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re
import unicodedata
from pathlib import Path

import cv2
import numpy as np
import pytesseract
import torch
from jiwer import cer as _cer, wer as _wer
from transformers import AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM, AutoTokenizer

from ..contracts import *  # noqa

def _cfg_get(cfg, section, key, default):
    return cfg.get(section, {}).get(key, default)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Tesseract reading
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def _crop(image_path: str, bbox: tuple[int, int, int, int]) -> np.ndarray:
    img = cv2.imread(image_path)
    if img is None:
        raise ValueError(f"OpenCV could not read {image_path}")
    x1, y1, x2, y2 = bbox
    h, w = img.shape[:2]
    x1, y1 = max(0, x1), max(0, y1)
    x2, y2 = min(w, x2), min(h, y2)
    return img[y1:y2, x1:x2]

def _tesseract_region(img_bgr: np.ndarray, lang: str, psm: int) -> str:
    rgb = cv2.cvtColor(img_bgr, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
    return pytesseract.image_to_string(rgb, lang=lang, config=f"--psm {psm}").strip()

def _split_lines(text: str) -> list[str]:
    return [ln.strip() for ln in text.splitlines() if ln.strip()]

def _normalize(text: str) -> str:
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text)
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# mT5 corrector -- lazy singleton, mirrors vision/layout.py's _get_model()
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

_CORRECTOR = None

class _Corrector:
    def __init__(self, checkpoint_path: str, max_length: int, num_threads: int | None):
        if num_threads:
            torch.set_num_threads(num_threads)
        self.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint_path)
        self.model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(checkpoint_path)
        self.model.to("cpu")
        self.model.eval()
        self.max_length = max_length
        self.prefix = "ocr_fix: "

    @torch.no_grad()
    def correct_batch(self, lines: list[str], batch_size: int = 32) -> list[str]:
        if not lines:
            return []
        out: list[str] = []
        for i in range(0, len(lines), batch_size):
            batch = lines[i:i + batch_size]
            inputs = self.tokenizer(
                [self.prefix + ln for ln in batch],
                return_tensors="pt", padding=True, truncation=True,
                max_length=self.max_length,
            )
            gen_ids = self.model.generate(**inputs, max_length=self.max_length, num_beams=1)
            out.extend(self.tokenizer.batch_decode(gen_ids, skip_special_tokens=True))
        return out

def _get_corrector(cfg: dict) -> "_Corrector":
    global _CORRECTOR
    if _CORRECTOR is None:
        checkpoint_path = cfg["ocr"]["corrector_checkpoint_path"]  # point this at checkpoint-2200
        max_length = int(_cfg_get(cfg, "ocr", "corrector_max_length", 96))
        num_threads = _cfg_get(cfg, "ocr", "corrector_cpu_threads", None)
        _CORRECTOR = _Corrector(checkpoint_path, max_length, num_threads)
    return _CORRECTOR

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Ground-truth lookup -- silently no-ops for real documents with no GT
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def _parse_page_id(page_id: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """loader.py builds Page.id as '<doc_id>:<page_stem>' -- split it back
    apart to locate the source image and the matching GT file."""
    doc_id, _, page_stem = page_id.partition(":")
    return doc_id, page_stem

def _load_gt_lines(gt_root: Path, doc_id: str, page_stem: str) -> list[str] | None:
    gt_path = gt_root / doc_id / f"{page_stem}.txt"
    if not gt_path.exists():
        return None
    with open(gt_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return _split_lines(f.read())

class _MetricAccumulator:
    def __init__(self, held_out_docs: set[str]):
        self.held_out_docs = held_out_docs
        self.all_hyp, self.all_ref = [], []
        self.held_hyp, self.held_ref = [], []

    def add(self, doc_id: str, hyp: str, ref: str):
        if not ref.strip():
            return
        self.all_hyp.append(hyp); self.all_ref.append(ref)
        if doc_id in self.held_out_docs:
            self.held_hyp.append(hyp); self.held_ref.append(ref)

    def report(self, label: str):
        def _scores(hyps, refs):
            return (_cer(refs, hyps), _wer(refs, hyps)) if refs else None
        corpus, held = _scores(self.all_hyp, self.all_ref), _scores(self.held_hyp, self.held_ref)
        print(f"\n=== {label} ===")
        print(f"corpus-wide : cer={corpus[0]:.4f}  wer={corpus[1]:.4f}  (n={len(self.all_ref)})"
              if corpus else "corpus-wide : no ground truth found -- skipped")
        print(f"held-out    : cer={held[0]:.4f}  wer={held[1]:.4f}  (n={len(self.held_ref)})"
              if held else "held-out    : no ground truth found -- skipped")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Main entry point
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

class Reader:
    """Kept for interface compatibility -- transcribe() below does the real work."""
    def __init__(self, cfg: dict) -> None:
        self.cfg = cfg["ocr"]

    def transcribe_region(self, region: Region) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError("use transcribe()")

def transcribe(regions: list[Region], cfg: dict) -> list[Chunk]:
    ocr_cfg = cfg.get("ocr", {})
    lang = ocr_cfg.get("tesseract_lang", "ben")  # ben+eng regressed corpus-wide CER 0.16->0.25 -- stay ben-only
    use_corrector = ocr_cfg.get("use_corrector", True)
    batch_size = int(ocr_cfg.get("corrector_batch_size", 32))
    data_root = Path(_cfg_get(cfg, "ingest", "data_root", "data"))
    pages_dir = _cfg_get(cfg, "ingest", "pages_dir", "pages")
    gt_root = data_root / ocr_cfg.get("gt_dir", "ground-truth-ocr")
    held_out_docs = set(ocr_cfg.get("held_out_docs", ["Krishi-Darpan"]))

    raw_metrics = _MetricAccumulator(held_out_docs)
    corrected_metrics = _MetricAccumulator(held_out_docs) if use_corrector else None

    # Pass 1: Tesseract per region, split into lines, flatten across the
    # WHOLE corpus so correction (pass 2) runs as large batches instead of
    # tiny per-region calls -- this is the main CPU-throughput lever.
    region_lines: list[list[str]] = []
    region_meta: list[tuple[Region, str, str]] = []
    flat_lines: list[str] = []
    flat_owner: list[tuple[int, int]] = []

    for region in regions:
        if region.kind == "figure":
            continue
        doc_id, page_stem = _parse_page_id(region.page_id)
        image_path = str(data_root / pages_dir / doc_id / f"{page_stem}.png")
        psm = 7 if region.kind == "heading" else 6
        crop = _crop(image_path, region.bbox)
        raw_text = _tesseract_region(crop, lang=lang, psm=psm)
        lines = [_normalize(ln) for ln in _split_lines(raw_text)]

        region_idx = len(region_lines)
        region_lines.append(lines)
        region_meta.append((region, doc_id, page_stem))
        for j, ln in enumerate(lines):
            flat_lines.append(ln)
            flat_owner.append((region_idx, j))

        gt_lines = _load_gt_lines(gt_root, doc_id, page_stem)
        if gt_lines:
            for j, ln in enumerate(lines):
                if j < len(gt_lines):
                    raw_metrics.add(doc_id, ln, _normalize(gt_lines[j]))

    # Pass 2: one batched correction sweep over every line in the corpus.
    if use_corrector and flat_lines:
        corrected_flat = _get_corrector(cfg).correct_batch(flat_lines, batch_size=batch_size)
    else:
        corrected_flat = flat_lines

    corrected_region_lines = [list(lines) for lines in region_lines]
    for (region_idx, line_idx), corrected in zip(flat_owner, corrected_flat):
        corrected_region_lines[region_idx][line_idx] = corrected

    # Pass 3: build chunks + corrected-side metrics.
    chunks: list[Chunk] = []
    for region_idx, (region, doc_id, page_stem) in enumerate(region_meta):
        lines = corrected_region_lines[region_idx]
        gt_lines = _load_gt_lines(gt_root, doc_id, page_stem)
        if corrected_metrics is not None and gt_lines:
            for j, ln in enumerate(lines):
                if j < len(gt_lines):
                    corrected_metrics.add(doc_id, ln, _normalize(gt_lines[j]))
        # NOTE: adjust field names if your actual Chunk (contracts.py) differs
        chunks.append(Chunk(page_id=region.page_id, bbox=region.bbox, kind=region.kind, text="\n".join(lines)))

    raw_metrics.report("Tesseract (raw)")
    if corrected_metrics is not None:
        corrected_metrics.report("Tesseract + mT5 corrector")

    return chunks

Config keys this expects under cfg["ocr"]:

ocr:
  tesseract_lang: "ben"
  use_corrector: true
  corrector_checkpoint_path: "/path/to/checkpoint-2200"   # not 2800
  corrector_max_length: 96
  corrector_batch_size: 32
  corrector_cpu_threads: null   # or an int matching your machine's cores
  gt_dir: "ground-truth-ocr"
  held_out_docs: ["Krishi-Darpan"]

"""FIXED data contracts. Do not change fields or types."""
from __future__ import annotations
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Page(BaseModel):
    id: str
    image_path: str
    doc_id: str

class Region(BaseModel):
    page_id: str
    bbox: tuple[int, int, int, int]
    kind: str  # text | table | figure | heading

class Chunk(BaseModel):
    id: str
    doc_id: str
    text: str
    page_ids: list[str]
    score: float = 0.0        # relevance score set by retrieval; decide() reads the top score to judge weak evidence

class Query(BaseModel):
    text: str
    verifiable: bool          # True = checkable by exact match (anchors objective grading + RLVR)
    judged: bool              # True = scored by LLM-judge / human (non-verifiable inference)

class Citation(BaseModel):
    chunk_id: str
    span: tuple[int, int]

class Answer(BaseModel):
    text: str
    citations: list[Citation]
    grounded: bool
    confidence: float

class ToolResult(BaseModel):
    ok: bool
    payload: dict

class TraceStep(BaseModel):
    """One agent step, emitted to traces/run.jsonl so the A3 agentic-feature check can read the path."""
    step: int
    tool: str                 # tool name, or "decide" / "answer"
    args: dict                # e.g. {"query": "..."} — for retrieve, the query actually used
    obs: dict                 # what decide() saw, e.g. {"top_score": 0.31, "n": 10}

# MANDATORY agentic behaviour (graded in A3): evidence-gated re-search — decide() must re-retrieve with a
# reformulated query when the top evidence is weak. That runtime branch is what makes the system an agent.
# (multi-hop -> recall NFR, verify-and-correct -> precision NFR, tool-routing -> bonus; see the codebase guide.)

Good catch to check — and yes, the real Chunk contract is meaningfully different from what I guessed last time (bbox/kind fields don't exist on it at all; it needs id, doc_id, page_ids as a list). That's a real bug in the code I gave you — here's the fix, plus the full trace of what happens to each region.

The region trace, region by region

ocr.transcribe(regions, cfg) receives every region layout.detect() found (pipeline.py doesn't pre-filter by kind — line-by-line: regions = layout.detect(...) then text = ocr.transcribe(regions, cfg) with nothing in between). So the filtering has to happen inside ocr.transcribe(), which is what the if region.kind == "figure": continue does. Tracing each kind from there:

text / table / heading → cropped, Tesseract'd, split into lines, corrected by mT5, become one Chunk each. Nothing dropped.

figure → skipped, deliberately — there's no text to OCR out of a photo/diagram. But look at layout.py's _NAME_TO_KIND: "figure_caption": "text". DocLayout-YOLO emits the figure's caption as its own separate region already tagged "text", not bundled into the "figure" region. So a figure's caption still flows through the pipeline as an ordinary text region — only the uncaptioned pixel content of the figure itself is (correctly) excluded.

So nothing is silently lost except image content that was never OCR-able to begin with. But don't take my word for it — the patch below adds an explicit region-accounting log so you can verify this from real output every run, not just trust my claim.

Fix: Chunk construction

Your actual contract:

class Chunk(BaseModel):
    id: str
    doc_id: str
    text: str
    page_ids: list[str]
    score: float = 0.0

No bbox, no kind — my earlier draft invented fields that don't exist and would fail Pydantic validation immediately. Replace the chunk-building section of the ocr.py I gave you with this (everything else — the Tesseract pass, the batched correction pass, the metrics accumulator — stays exactly as before):

def _region_chunk_id(region: Region) -> str:
    """Deterministic id from page_id + bbox -- stable across re-runs on the
    same layout output, since Region carries no id of its own."""
    x1, y1, x2, y2 = region.bbox
    return f"{region.page_id}:{x1}-{y1}-{x2}-{y2}"

# Pass 3: build chunks + corrected-side metrics.
chunks: list[Chunk] = []
kind_counts: dict[str, int] = {}
skipped_figures = 0

for region in regions:
    kind_counts[region.kind] = kind_counts.get(region.kind, 0) + 1
    if region.kind == "figure":
        skipped_figures += 1

for region_idx, (region, doc_id, page_stem) in enumerate(region_meta):
    lines = corrected_region_lines[region_idx]
    gt_lines = _load_gt_lines(gt_root, doc_id, page_stem)
    if corrected_metrics is not None and gt_lines:
        for j, ln in enumerate(lines):
            if j < len(gt_lines):
                corrected_metrics.add(doc_id, ln, _normalize(gt_lines[j]))
    chunks.append(Chunk(
        id=_region_chunk_id(region),
        doc_id=doc_id,
        text="\n".join(lines),
        page_ids=[region.page_id],
        score=0.0,
    ))

print(f"\n=== Region accounting ===")
print(f"input regions by kind : {kind_counts}")
print(f"figures skipped (no text to extract) : {skipped_figures}")
print(f"chunks emitted : {len(chunks)}  "
      f"(expected = input regions - figures = {sum(kind_counts.values()) - skipped_figures})")
if len(chunks) != sum(kind_counts.values()) - skipped_figures:
    print("WARNING: chunk count doesn't match expected -- a region was dropped somewhere above")

raw_metrics.report("Tesseract (raw)")
if corrected_metrics is not None:
    corrected_metrics.report("Tesseract + mT5 corrector")

return chunks

The warning at the end is the safety net for your actual concern — if any future edit to the region loop accidentally drops one, this will tell you immediately instead of silently shipping a gap.

One open question I can't resolve without seeing chunk.py: pipeline.py does hooks.run(hooks.AFTER_OCR, {"chunks": text}) — labeling stage 3's raw output "chunks" — then immediately calls chunks = chunk.split(text, cfg) on that same value. That strongly implies chunk.split() expects list[Chunk] as input (one per region, as built above) and performs the real merging/splitting logic — e.g. combining adjacent same-page regions into embedding-sized windows, assigning final ids, deciding whether text/table/heading chunks get merged or kept separate. I've deliberately kept OCR's output at one-chunk-per-region granularity (the finest reasonable unit) rather than guessing at any merging logic myself, since that decision belongs to stage 4, not stage 3 — worth confirming chunk.split() actually treats its input this way before you run the full pipeline.

Architected debug filtering and timing instrumentation for isolated OCR testing.

Done

Good instinct — the fix is a debug cap that caps pages after blank-page filtering (so you're guaranteed real content) but before layout runs (since that's your actual bottleneck), plus per-stage timing so you don't have to guess where time is going. I've also added throughput logging inside the corrector itself, since "does mT5 run fast enough" is really "what's the lines/sec rate," and that number extrapolates cleanly to your full corpus without needing a full run.

pipeline.py — add debug cap + stage timing

Stage order and every hooks.run()/register_all() call stay exactly where they were — this only wraps each call in a timer and inserts one filtering line between preprocess and enhance.

"""FIXED end-to-end order (Stages 0-9) + cross-cutting seams.
Do not reorder stages or remove hooks.run()/register_all() calls."""
from __future__ import annotations
import time
from . import config, hooks, wiring  # noqa: F401
from .ingest import loader, preprocess, enhance
from .vision import layout, ocr
from .index import chunk, embed, store
from .retrieval import retriever
from .agent import agent
from .contracts import Page

def _apply_debug_limits(pages: list[Page], cfg: dict) -> list[Page]:
    """Dev/debug speed knob -- caps how many pages flow into layout + OCR
    so you can smoke-test the pipeline without waiting on the full corpus.
    No-op unless cfg['debug']['max_pages_per_doc'] is set. Optionally
    restrict to specific books via cfg['debug']['doc_ids'] (useful for
    testing specifically on the held-out book, e.g. Krishi-Darpan)."""
    debug_cfg = cfg.get("debug", {})
    max_per_doc = debug_cfg.get("max_pages_per_doc")
    doc_ids = debug_cfg.get("doc_ids")

    if doc_ids:
        pages = [p for p in pages if p.doc_id in doc_ids]

    if not max_per_doc:
        if doc_ids:
            print(f"[debug] doc_ids={doc_ids} active -- {len(pages)} pages")
        return pages

    by_doc: dict[str, list[Page]] = {}
    for p in pages:
        by_doc.setdefault(p.doc_id, []).append(p)
    limited = [p for doc_pages in by_doc.values() for p in doc_pages[:max_per_doc]]
    print(f"[debug] max_pages_per_doc={max_per_doc} doc_ids={doc_ids or 'all'} "
          f"-- using {len(limited)}/{len(pages)} pages")
    return limited

def _timed(label: str, fn, *args, **kwargs):
    start = time.time()
    result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
    print(f"[timing] {label}: {time.time() - start:.1f}s")
    return result

def build_knowledge_base(cfg: dict) -> None:
    wiring.register_all(cfg)                        # wire cross-cutting features
    pages = _timed("loader.load_pages", loader.load_pages, cfg)
    pages = _timed("preprocess.run", preprocess.run, pages, cfg)
    pages = _apply_debug_limits(pages, cfg)          # <-- debug cap, applied after blank-page filtering
    pages = _timed("enhance.run", enhance.run, pages, cfg)
    hooks.run(hooks.AFTER_INGEST, {"pages": pages})
    regions = _timed("layout.detect", layout.detect, pages, cfg)             # Stage 2
    text = _timed("ocr.transcribe", ocr.transcribe, regions, cfg)             # Stage 3
    hooks.run(hooks.AFTER_OCR, {"chunks": text})    # e.g. PII redaction on extracted text
    chunks = _timed("chunk.split", chunk.split, text, cfg)                 # Stage 4
    hooks.run(hooks.BEFORE_INDEX, {"chunks": chunks})
    vectors = _timed("embed.encode", embed.encode, chunks, cfg)
    store.build(chunks, vectors, cfg)

def answer(query_text: str, cfg: dict):
    wiring.register_all(cfg)
    r = retriever.Retriever(cfg)                    # Stage 5
    return agent.Agent(cfg, r).run(query_text)      # Stage 6 (seams run inside the loop)

One tradeoff worth knowing: preprocess.run() still scans all pages before the cap kicks in (it needs to, to guarantee your debug subset is real non-blank content). That's fine — the connected-components check it does is cheap OpenCV, not the bottleneck. If it ever does become slow, moving _apply_debug_limits to right after loader.load_pages instead trades that guarantee for extra speed.

ocr.py — add throughput logging

Three small additions to the version from before; everything else in the file is unchanged.

import time  # add to imports at the top

In _Corrector.__init__, time the (one-time) model load separately from per-line throughput:

def __init__(self, checkpoint_path: str, max_length: int, num_threads: int | None):
        if num_threads:
            torch.set_num_threads(num_threads)
        start = time.time()
        self.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint_path)
        self.model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(checkpoint_path)
        self.model.to("cpu")
        self.model.eval()
        print(f"[timing] mT5 corrector loaded in {time.time() - start:.1f}s "
              f"(one-time cost -- excluded from per-line rate below)")
        self.max_length = max_length
        self.prefix = "ocr_fix: "

In correct_batch, report the actual lines/sec rate — this is the number to extrapolate from:

@torch.no_grad()
    def correct_batch(self, lines: list[str], batch_size: int = 32) -> list[str]:
        if not lines:
            return []
        start = time.time()
        out: list[str] = []
        for i in range(0, len(lines), batch_size):
            batch = lines[i:i + batch_size]
            inputs = self.tokenizer(
                [self.prefix + ln for ln in batch],
                return_tensors="pt", padding=True, truncation=True,
                max_length=self.max_length,
            )
            gen_ids = self.model.generate(**inputs, max_length=self.max_length, num_beams=1)
            out.extend(self.tokenizer.batch_decode(gen_ids, skip_special_tokens=True))
        elapsed = time.time() - start
        rate = len(lines) / elapsed if elapsed > 0 else float("inf")
        print(f"[timing] correction: {len(lines)} lines in {elapsed:.1f}s ({rate:.1f} lines/sec)")
        return out

In transcribe(), wrap the Tesseract pass (pass 1) the same way — put this around the for region in regions: loop:

t_pass1 = time.time()
    for region in regions:
        # ... unchanged body ...
        pass
    print(f"[timing] tesseract pass: {len(region_meta)} regions, "
          f"{len(flat_lines)} lines in {time.time() - t_pass1:.1f}s")

Running the smoke test

Wherever cfg gets built for run_ingest.py (your YAML config or wherever it's assembled before build_knowledge_base(cfg) is called), add:

debug:
  doc_ids: ["Krishi-Darpan"]   # test on the held-out book specifically
  max_pages_per_doc: 5

This gets you both answers fast: [timing] layout.detect tells you whether layout itself is the slow part (YOLO inference is the likely suspect, since it's the only deep-model stage before OCR), and the corrector's lines/sec print tells you your real CPU throughput — multiply that against your actual full-corpus line count (from a completed run's log, since this pipeline's per-region line splits may differ somewhat from your original ~16k doctr-aligned line dataset) to get an honest full-corpus estimate before committing to it.

Two more independent levers already in your config if you want to isolate further: use_corrector: false isolates raw-Tesseract-only timing, and dropping max_pages_per_doc (or setting it to null) turns the debug cap off entirely for the real run.

Diagnosed alignment bug and architected page-level metrics restructuring.

Root cause of the unreal numbers: it's the region-to-GT matching, not the model. Look at your own log — page-004 alone produced 3 titles + 6 plain texts = 9 separate text/heading regions. But transcribe()'s scoring does for j, ln in enumerate(lines): raw_metrics.add(doc_id, ln, gt_lines[j]) inside the per-region loop — meaning every region's line index resets to j=0 and gets compared against gt_lines[0], gt_lines[1], ... of the whole page again. Nine unrelated regions all get scored against the same opening handful of GT lines. That alone explains CER≈0.95/WER≈1.21 (WER>1 is the signature of an insertion-heavy, totally scrambled alignment).

The corrected pass being worse (CER 13.6!) is a secondary, explainable effect of the same root cause: fed a tiny, already-mismatched fragment (e.g. a 1-2 word "abandon" header/page-number scrap), the corrector's greedy decoding (num_beams=1) can degenerate into a long repetition loop — the exact failure mode you saw early in training on out-of-distribution input. jiwer.cer has no upper bound; a long hallucinated output scored against a short wrongly-matched reference produces exactly this kind of blowup.

Fix: replace the naive per-region positional zip with a per-page DP alignment (the same approach you used to build the training set originally) — group every region's lines by page in reading order, align the whole page's hypothesis lines against that page's GT lines once, then score both raw and corrected passes off the same alignment (correction never changes line count/order, so one alignment serves both).

ocr.py — changes

Add near the top, alongside the other helper functions:

def _align_lines_to_gt(hyp_lines: list[str], gt_lines: list[str], skip_cost: float = 0.75) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    """Monotonic DP alignment (Needleman-Wunsch style) between a page's hypothesis
    lines and its GT lines, CER as substitution cost. Necessary because OCR regions
    rarely produce one line per GT line -- a naive positional zip compares unrelated
    regions against the same early GT lines and produces nonsensical error rates."""
    n, m = len(hyp_lines), len(gt_lines)
    if n == 0 or m == 0:
        return []
    cost = [[_cer(gt_lines[j], hyp_lines[i]) if gt_lines[j].strip() else 1.0
             for j in range(m)] for i in range(n)]
    dp = [[0.0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    back = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        dp[i][0] = dp[i - 1][0] + skip_cost; back[i][0] = 1
    for j in range(1, m + 1):
        dp[0][j] = dp[0][j - 1] + skip_cost; back[0][j] = 2
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(1, m + 1):
            match_c = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + cost[i - 1][j - 1]
            skip_h, skip_g = dp[i - 1][j] + skip_cost, dp[i][j - 1] + skip_cost
            best = min(match_c, skip_h, skip_g)
            dp[i][j] = best
            back[i][j] = 0 if best == match_c else (1 if best == skip_h else 2)
    i, j, pairs = n, m, []
    while i > 0 or j > 0:
        move = back[i][j]
        if i > 0 and j > 0 and move == 0:
            pairs.append((i - 1, j - 1)); i -= 1; j -= 1
        elif i > 0 and (j == 0 or move == 1):
            i -= 1
        else:
            j -= 1
    pairs.reverse()
    return pairs

In transcribe(), sort regions by page + reading order first (add right after the config lines, before pass 1):

        if gt_lines:
            for j, ln in enumerate(lines):
                if j < len(gt_lines):
                    raw_metrics.add(doc_id, ln, _normalize(gt_lines[j]))

Insert this new step right after pass 2 (correction), before pass 3 (chunk building):

# Pass 2.5: page-grouped DP alignment -- one alignment per page, reused
    # for both raw and corrected scoring since correction preserves line order.
    pages_order: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
    page_region_idxs: dict[tuple[str, str], list[int]] = {}
    for idx, (region, doc_id, page_stem) in enumerate(region_meta):
        key = (doc_id, page_stem)
        if key not in page_region_idxs:
            page_region_idxs[key] = []
            pages_order.append(key)
        page_region_idxs[key].append(idx)

    for doc_id, page_stem in pages_order:
        idxs = page_region_idxs[(doc_id, page_stem)]
        page_raw = [ln for i in idxs for ln in region_lines[i]]
        page_corrected = [ln for i in idxs for ln in corrected_region_lines[i]]
        gt_lines = _load_gt_lines(gt_root, doc_id, page_stem)
        if not gt_lines:
            continue
        gt_lines = [_normalize(g) for g in gt_lines]
        pairs = _align_lines_to_gt(page_raw, gt_lines)
        for hyp_idx, gt_idx in pairs:
            raw_metrics.add(doc_id, page_raw[hyp_idx], gt_lines[gt_idx])
            if corrected_metrics is not None:
                corrected_metrics.add(doc_id, page_corrected[hyp_idx], gt_lines[gt_idx])

And remove the now-duplicate scoring block from pass 3 (the if corrected_metrics is not None and gt_lines: chunk inside the pass-3 loop) — it's handled above now.

New file debug_log.py (same level as pipeline.py):

"""Routes verbose diagnostic output to a file when debug.log_file is set,
so the terminal stays readable during smoke tests. No-op (prints normally)
when not configured."""
from __future__ import annotations
import time
from pathlib import Path

_log_path: Path | None = None

def configure(cfg: dict) -> None:
    global _log_path
    log_file = cfg.get("debug", {}).get("log_file")
    _log_path = Path(log_file) if log_file else None
    if _log_path:
        _log_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        _log_path.write_text(f"=== debug run started {time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')} ===\n")

def log(msg: str) -> None:
    if _log_path is None:
        print(msg)
        return
    with open(_log_path, "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(msg + "\n")

8/13/2026 18:04:30

Can you explain the problem - where it was introduced - and how you are planning to solve it in brief?

Assistant:

8/13/2026 18:04:35

The problem: each page produced several separate OCR regions (e.g. page-004: 3 titles + 6 plain texts = 9 regions), but each region's lines were scored against the GT starting from index 0 every time — so region 2's lines got compared to the page's opening lines again, region 3's did too, and so on. Every region after the first was being checked against the wrong part of the page. That's a pure line-index bug: it was introduced the moment scoring moved from your original per-line training pipeline (one image = one line = one GT string, no ambiguity) to this per-region pipeline (one region = many lines, several regions per page) without re-deriving which GT lines each region's lines actually correspond to.

The fix: stop scoring inside the per-region loop. Instead, collect all lines from all regions on a page, in reading order, then run one page-level sequence alignment (the same DP approach used to build your original training set) between that full list and the page's GT lines. This finds the real correspondence regardless of how the page got split into regions, and both the raw and corrected passes reuse the same alignment since correction doesn't change line order or count.

@torch.no_grad()
    def correct_batch(self, lines: list[str], batch_size: int = 32) -> list[str]:
        if not lines:
            return []
        start = time.time()
        out: list[str] = []
        for i in range(0, len(lines), batch_size):
            batch = lines[i:i + batch_size]
            print("\n--- BEFORE correction ---")
            for ln in batch:
                print(repr(ln))
            inputs = self.tokenizer(
                [self.prefix + ln for ln in batch],
                return_tensors="pt", padding=True, truncation=True,
                max_length=self.max_length,
            )
            gen_ids = self.model.generate(**inputs, max_length=self.max_length, num_beams=1)
            decoded = self.tokenizer.batch_decode(gen_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
            print("--- AFTER correction ---")
            for ln in decoded:
                print(repr(ln))
            out.extend(decoded)
        elapsed = time.time() - start
        rate = len(lines) / elapsed if elapsed > 0 else float("inf")
        print(f"[timing] correction: {len(lines)} lines in {elapsed:.1f}s ({rate:.1f} lines/sec)")
        return out

Rerun on the 1 page — raw should already be trustworthy, and this will confirm whether corrected drops to something sane once the duplicate scoring is gone.

Diagnosed corrupted checkpoint weights and misaligned model loading configuration.

Done

The tell is in your directory listing, not the correction output. rng_state, scheduler, and training_args should each be a single file (rng_state.pth, scheduler.pt, training_args.bin) — but you're seeing them as folders containing byteorder, data.pkl, data/0, data/1, version. That's not a normal save format — that's literally the unzipped internal contents of a PyTorch checkpoint file. PyTorch's .pt/.pth/.bin files are zip archives internally; something in the Kaggle upload/download/packaging chain auto-extracted every zip archive it found in the output directory, turning each checkpoint file into a directory of its own guts.

That's strong circumstantial evidence the same thing may have damaged model.safetensors — not because safetensors is a zip (it isn't, so it wouldn't get "unzipped" the same way), but because whatever process did this clearly mangled the checkpoint directory, and you can't assume just one file was affected. Garbage repeated-foreign-subword output with num_beams=1 is exactly what you get from a model with corrupted or randomly-initialized weights — greedy decoding on broken weights collapses into looping the highest-probability token, which is what you're seeing.

Fastest way to confirm — load the checkpoint alone, outside the pipeline, and watch for load warnings:

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM

path = "mt5-small-2200"  # your actual local path
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(path)
model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(path)

If weights failed to load properly, from_pretrained prints something like:

Some weights of MT5ForConditionalGeneration were not initialized from the model checkpoint ... and are newly initialized: [...]
You should probably TRAIN this model on a down-stream task...

If you see that warning (or any warning at all here), that's your answer — the checkpoint didn't load into the model correctly, full stop.

Then test it in isolation, bypassing ocr.py entirely:

inputs = tokenizer("ocr_fix: কষি - বিজঞান", return_tensors="pt")
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_length=32, num_beams=1)
print(tokenizer.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True))

If this alone produces garbage, the checkpoint itself is bad — not your ocr.py code, not the pipeline, not the alignment fix. If it produces sensible Bengali, the bug is somewhere in how ocr.py resolves corrator_checkpoint_path (e.g. it's silently falling through to a cached base google/mt5-small because the configured path is wrong or unset) — worth printing the resolved path in _get_corrector to rule that out too.

Fix, once confirmed: re-download from Kaggle and check the file sizes against what your training notebook actually wrote (your last completed run's Kaggle output logs, or the sizes you quoted earlier — safetensors should land close to 2.23GB). If the re-download still shows the same corrupted directory structure, the problem is in how the notebook's output got zipped/packaged as a Kaggle dataset in the first place — try re-uploading the checkpoint as a fresh dataset version rather than trusting the existing one, and confirm the re-uploaded version's model.safetensors size matches before pulling it down again.

Both snippets now produce garbage — batching is exonerated (dropping it wouldn't have exposed this any faster, but at least that theory's closed). No missing-weights warning either, meaning from_pretrained believes every key it needed was present and correctly shaped. So the checkpoint isn't structurally corrupt, and it isn't a dtype/CPU issue — this points at a subtler kind of load-time corruption: the values landing in the wrong slot.

There's a real clue sitting in your own training log that I skipped over earlier. Right when the fresh google/mt5-small was first loaded (Cell 11), transformers printed:

The tied weights mapping and config for this model specifies to tie shared.weight to encoder.embed_tokens.weight, but both are present in the checkpoints, so we will NOT tie them.

mT5 is supposed to share one embedding matrix across the encoder input, decoder input, and the LM output head — three roles, one tensor. That message says your training environment's transformers version found four separate tensors already present and refused to tie them. That's non-default behavior for this model family, and it's a strong sign that whatever transformers version ran on Kaggle (your install cell pinned no upper bound: transformers>=4.40, so it grabbed whatever's current today) handles T5-style weight tying differently from the version pinned locally (>=4.40,<4.45 in your pyproject.toml).

Here's why that matters for you specifically: if the save side wrote out lm_head.weight as a real tensor (because it wasn't tied during training) but the load side's tie-detection logic behaves differently and re-ties lm_head to shared.weight anyway — or vice versa, expects a tied checkpoint and gets confused by four separate tensors — the model can end up generating from an embedding table that was never actually trained on OCR correction. Correct shapes, no missing-key warning, completely wrong values. That's exactly consistent with what you're seeing: real mT5 subword fragments (ILLAR, Blender, thesis) — so the vocabulary itself is intact — just decoded through what's effectively an untrained or mismatched output head.

Test this directly, in isolation:

import transformers
print("transformers version:", transformers.__version__)

from transformers import AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM
model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained("mt5-small-2200")

import torch
lm_head = model.lm_head.weight
shared = model.shared.weight if hasattr(model, "shared") else model.get_input_embeddings().weight

print("lm_head vs shared -- identical tensor?", lm_head.data_ptr() == shared.data_ptr())
print("lm_head vs shared -- allclose (values)?", torch.allclose(lm_head, shared))
print("lm_head std:", lm_head.std().item(), " shared std:", shared.std().item())

What to look for: if lm_head and shared are not close and lm_head's std is suspiciously small/uniform (near mT5's default init scale rather than matching shared's trained distribution), that confirms the head is untrained. If they are identical/tied, the bug is elsewhere and this theory is wrong — tell me the printed values either way, that fully decides it.

If it confirms the mismatch, the real fix isn't a code patch to ocr.py — it's pinning the exact same transformers version for loading that Kaggle used for saving. Run import transformers; print(transformers.__version__) in a fresh cell on Kaggle (or check the pip install log at the top of your notebook output) and match that version exactly in your local .venv, rather than relying on the <4.45 range in pyproject.toml.

lm_head and shared being bit-for-bit identical rules that theory out completely — the embeddings aren't corrupted or mistied. Good, that narrows things a lot. A std of ~14 isn't inherently alarming for T5-family embeddings (unlike BERT, T5 has no LayerNorm right after the embedding lookup, so larger scale is normal) — so nothing here points at damaged weights anymore.

That shifts suspicion from "the weights are wrong" to "the weights are fine but generate() is starting the decoder from the wrong place." mT5's autoregressive decoding is entirely dependent on decoder_start_token_id being correct — if that ID is subtly wrong (present in the checkpoint's generation_config.json, but set incorrectly, e.g. from a version-dependent default that changed between whatever produced this checkpoint and 4.44.2 locally), the very first token fed to the decoder is out-of-distribution, and everything downstream compounds through autoregression — degenerate repeated fragments like ILLARILLARILLAR... is a textbook signature of exactly this, not of bad weights.

The decisive test — bypass generate() entirely and check if the trained weights predict correctly under teacher forcing, using one of your own verified training-log pairs:

import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM

path = "mt5-small-2200"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(path)
model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(path)
model.eval()

# from your own cell 17 output -- known correct pair
hyp = "ocr_fix: আসিবে । ইহা দ্বারাই বুঝ! যায় যে, উদ্ভিদ আলোক অনুভব করিয়া"
gt  = "আসিবে। ইহা দ্বারাই বুঝা যায় যে, উদ্ভিদ আলোক অনুভব করিয়া"

inputs = tokenizer(hyp, return_tensors="pt")
labels = tokenizer(text_target=gt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids

with torch.no_grad():
    out = model(**inputs, labels=labels)

print("loss:", out.loss.item())  # should be LOW (well under 1) if weights are intact
pred_ids = out.logits.argmax(-1)
print("teacher-forced greedy decode:", tokenizer.decode(pred_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True))

# now compare against decoder_start_token_id actually in play
print("model.generation_config.decoder_start_token_id:", model.generation_config.decoder_start_token_id)
print("model.config.decoder_start_token_id:", model.config.decoder_start_token_id)
print("tokenizer.pad_token_id:", tokenizer.pad_token_id)
print("correct T5 default is pad_token_id:", tokenizer.pad_token_id)

Two outcomes:

Loss is low (well under 1) and the teacher-forced decode looks like real Bengali close to GT → the weights are completely intact, and the bug is purely in how generate() seeds the decoder. The fix is forcing the correct start token explicitly:

out = model.generate(**inputs, max_length=96, num_beams=1,
                      decoder_start_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id)

If that alone fixes it, add decoder_start_token_id explicitly wherever ocr.py calls generate(), rather than trusting the checkpoint's generation_config.json.

Loss is high / teacher-forced decode is also garbage → the weights themselves genuinely aren't the trained ones, and we're back to a save/load corruption question — at that point the next move is re-verifying the Kaggle-side transformers version against your local 4.44.2, since that's still the most likely place a T5-family default could silently diverge between save and load.

Run this and tell me the loss value and what the teacher-forced decode looks like — that one number settles which branch we're in.

That loss number is the decisive piece, and it points somewhere more specific than "generic bad checkpoint." For mT5-small's 250k-token vocabulary, a uniformly random model would score cross-entropy loss around ln(250112) ≈ 12.4. You're at 31.66 — more than double that. A model can only exceed the random-guess baseline by confidently predicting the wrong token, not by being merely untrained or randomly initialized. Combined with that unusually large embedding std (14, and since T5 ties its embedding matrix directly into the output projection with no extra scaling layer, an oversized embedding norm directly produces oversized, overconfident, wrong logits) — this looks like scale-corrupted or otherwise altered tensor values, not a structurally broken or untrained checkpoint.

Here's the logical lever that actually narrows this down: cells 17 and 18, in that same Kaggle session, used this exact trained model — post-load_best_model_at_end, i.e. checkpoint-2200's weights — and produced good results (CER 0.114 on held-out Darpan, sane corrections). That means the trained weights themselves are fine. So the corruption isn't in training — it's specifically in one of two places: (a) what Trainer wrote to checkpoint-2200/model.safetensors on disk during training didn't match what was in memory, or (b) something altered the file's bytes during Kaggle's packaging/upload or your download.

This is checkable directly, without guessing further:

Step 1 — checksum both ends, to isolate transfer corruption:

Locally:

shasum -a 256 mt5-small-2200/model.safetensors

In a fresh Kaggle notebook cell (new session, don't retrain — just read the file that's sitting in your Kaggle output/dataset):

import hashlib
with open("checkpoint-2200/model.safetensors", "rb") as f:
    print(hashlib.sha256(f.read()).hexdigest())

If these two hashes don't match, it's a download/packaging corruption — re-download fixes it outright.

Step 2 — if the hashes DO match, the corruption happened at save-time on Kaggle itself, meaning it's baked into the file before it ever left Kaggle. Test that directly, still in a fresh Kaggle session, no training involved — load straight from the on-disk checkpoint and rerun your loss/decode test from before:

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM
import torch

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("checkpoint-2200")
model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained("checkpoint-2200")

hyp = "ocr_fix: আসিবে । ইহা দ্বারাই বুঝ! যায় যে, উদ্ভিদ আলোক অনুভব করিয়া"
gt  = "আসিবে। ইহা দ্বারাই বুঝা যায় যে, উদ্ভিদ আলোক অনুভব করিয়া"
inputs = tokenizer(hyp, return_tensors="pt")
labels = tokenizer(text_target=gt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
with torch.no_grad():
    out = model(**inputs, labels=labels)

If this also comes back ~30+ on Kaggle itself, freshly loaded from disk, that confirms the save step is the actual culprit — the in-memory post-training model and what Trainer.save_model() wrote to that checkpoint directory have diverged. If it comes back low (matching cell 17/18's real quality), then step 1's hashes must not have matched and you're purely dealing with a transfer issue.

Parallel low-cost move while you run this: you already have checkpoint-2800 saved too — run the same loss test on it. If 2800 is also garbage, that's strong evidence this is systemic to how checkpoints are being saved/exported in general (worth suspecting save_total_limit=2 combined with the mid-training checkpoint deletion/rotation, or a Kaggle-specific output-syncing quirk), not something specific to the 2200 file. If 2800 loads clean and scores low loss, that isolates the problem to something that specifically happened during the 2200 save event, and 2800 becomes your working deployment checkpoint in the meantime.

That's very likely it, and it fits everything you've seen. A 2.23GB file downloaded through a browser's per-file download button (rather than a resumable, integrity-checked transfer) is exactly the kind of operation that can silently produce a file of the correct final size but with corrupted bytes in the middle — a dropped connection that resumes from the wrong offset, an interrupted download the browser "completes" from a stale partial, etc. That would explain precisely what you're seeing: safetensors' header still parses fine (so no shape/missing-key errors), but the actual float values are scrambled — consistent with your loss being 31.66 (worse than random, not just untrained) and the output being incoherent multi-script garbage rather than plausible Bengali.

One thing worth naming directly: you never needed optimizer.pt (4.45GB) at all — we established a while back that inference only needs config.json, generation_config.json, model.safetensors, tokenizer_config.json, spiece.model/tokenizer.json, special_tokens_map.json. That means the disk-space pressure that pushed you toward manual one-by-one browser downloads was partly unnecessary — skipping the optimizer file alone frees ~4.45GB per checkpoint, which likely removes the constraint entirely.

Redo the download this way instead, for checkpoint-2200 only (your best checkpoint — no need to also pull 2800 unless this one still fails):

If you have the Kaggle CLI set up:

kaggle datasets download -d <your-dataset-slug> -f checkpoint-2200/model.safetensors -p ./mt5-small-2200/

(substitute your actual dataset slug — this pulls just that one file, and the CLI handles the transfer more robustly than a browser click for a file this size)

If you don't have the CLI configured, at minimum re-download model.safetensors again through the browser (sometimes a second attempt succeeds where the first silently didn't), and do not trust it until you verify it — run the same checksum check from before immediately after, before touching transformers at all:

shasum -a 256 mt5-small-2200/model.safetensors

against the hash from a fresh Kaggle cell:

import hashlib
with open("checkpoint-2200/model.safetensors", "rb") as f:
    print(hashlib.sha256(f.read()).hexdigest())

Only once those two hashes match should you rerun the loss test from before (out.loss.item() — expecting well under 1, not 31). If they match and the loss is still bad, we're back to the save-time corruption branch from my last message; if they match and the loss comes back low, this was the answer and you're clear to plug the checkpoint back into ocr.py.

Confirmed, and it's not the optimizer file — it's the transformers version. Same file, same hash, same weights: loss 0.0012 (correct) under transformers 5.0.0, loss 31.66 (garbage) under 4.44.2. That's a 4.x→5.0 major-version jump, and mT5's known ambiguity is the prime suspect: your checkpoint's config.json says the input/output embeddings should be tied (tie_word_embeddings=True, mT5's default), but the actual .safetensors file stores shared.weight, encoder.embed_tokens.weight, decoder.embed_tokens.weight, and lm_head.weight as four separate real tensors (we confirmed their values are identical, but they're stored as distinct tensors, not aliased). The load-time warning even tells you this is ambiguous: "the config...specifies to tie...but both are present...we will NOT tie them. You should update the config with tie_word_embeddings=False". T5-family models apply a scaling step to the decoder output before the LM head only when tie_word_embeddings=True — if 4.44.2 and 5.0.0 resolve this tied/untied ambiguity differently at the point that scaling decision gets made, one version applies a compensation the weights were never trained under, and the other doesn't. That mismatch alone is enough to produce exactly what you're seeing: correct-shaped, correct-valued weights driving a completely different computation.

from tqdm import tqdm  # add to imports at the top, alongside cv2/pytesseract/etc.

Pass 1 (Tesseract) — wrap the region loop:

t_pass1 = time.time()
    regions = sorted(regions, key=lambda r: (r.page_id, r.bbox[1], r.bbox[0]))
    for region in tqdm(regions, desc="tesseract"):
        if region.kind == "figure":
            continue
        ...  # rest of the loop body unchanged

Pass 2 (correction) — inside correct_batch, wrap the batch loop. Since debugging's done, this is also a good moment to drop the BEFORE/AFTER print block (it'll otherwise print through/over the bar on every batch):

@torch.no_grad()
    def correct_batch(self, lines: list[str], batch_size: int = 32) -> list[str]:
        if not lines:
            return []
        start = time.time()
        out: list[str] = []
        n_batches = (len(lines) + batch_size - 1) // batch_size
        for i in tqdm(range(0, len(lines), batch_size), total=n_batches, desc="mt5 correct"):
            batch = lines[i:i + batch_size]
            inputs = self.tokenizer(
                [self.prefix + ln for ln in batch],
                return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, padding=True,
                max_length=self.max_length,
            )
            gen_ids = self.model.generate(**inputs, max_length=self.max_length, num_beams=1)
            out.extend(self.tokenizer.batch_decode(gen_ids, skip_special_tokens=True))
        elapsed = time.time() - start
        rate = len(lines) / elapsed if elapsed > 0 else float("inf")
        print(f"[timing] correction: {len(lines)} lines in {elapsed:.1f}s ({rate:.1f} lines/sec)")
        return out

That gives you two live bars in sequence — region count for Tesseract, batch count for mT5 — each showing rate and ETA, without needing tqdm.auto since you're running from a plain terminal, not a notebook.

Assistant:

8/13/2026 21:45:14

Analyzed metric divergence between character and word error rates.

Analyzed metric divergence between character and word error rates.

Done

Yes — it's not just normal, it's the expected signature of this specific corrector, and there's a concrete mechanism behind it:

CER and WER measure different things. WER only asks "is this whole word right or wrong?" — fixing one wrong character in an 8-character word turns a 1-word error into 0 errors, a full WER win, even though the character-level damage was tiny. CER counts every character precisely, so that same fix barely moves it. Meanwhile, if the corrector badly mangles one line — like the bracketed-English hallucination pattern we already found ((Root hair) → (CaCOnnual)) — that single line can carry a large edit distance (many wrong characters) while still only counting as one bad "word" for WER purposes elsewhere. So it's entirely possible for the corrector to turn several near-miss words into exact matches (big WER win) while one hallucinated line inflates the character-level tally (small CER loss) — net: WER drops a lot, CER ticks up slightly.

But the bigger factor here is your sample size: n=10. jiwer.cer/jiwer.wer compute corpus-level ratios (total edit distance ÷ total reference length), not per-line averages — so with only 10 aligned lines, a single line's outcome can swing the aggregate substantially. That's a direct consequence of debug.max_pages_per_doc: 1 — useful for confirming the pipeline runs end-to-end without errors, but not remotely enough data to draw a real conclusion about whether the corrector is actually net-positive here.

Don't read into these specific numbers. Bump max_pages_per_doc up (or drop it entirely for a real book-level run) before trusting the CER/WER comparison — the corpus-wide numbers from your Kaggle run (CER 0.114 vs raw 0.128, WER 0.303 vs raw 0.439, both improved, on 4,361 lines) are the trustworthy reference point, not this 10-line smoke test.
